title: Knee Abnormality Detection AI Challenge Overview

messages.text:
**Courtesy of Dr. Jacob Kazam**

## Overview of the Clinical Problem

The 2026 RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection AI Challenge asks participants to build machine learning models that detect a defined set of clinically important abnormalities on knee MRI examinations. It is the first RSNA AI Challenge to pair every imaging study with the text of its original radiology report, and to do so across a large, multilingual, international dataset. Models may learn from both the images and the report text, reflecting how knee MRI is actually interpreted and communicated in clinical practice.

The knee is one of the most frequently injured and most frequently imaged joints in the body. Knee disorders are a major and growing cause of pain and disability worldwide, affecting athletes, manual workers, and older adults alike. The knee is the most common site of osteoarthritis, which affects nearly a quarter of adults aged 40 and older, an estimated 654 million people worldwide. Acute injuries are also common: knee injuries account for an estimated 15 to 40 percent of all sports-related injuries.

Several structures are commonly involved. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears are among the most frequent sports injuries, often occurring during sudden pivots or changes of direction and leading to immediate instability. Medial collateral ligament (MCL) injuries typically result from outward (valgus) stress on the knee and frequently accompany other structural damage. Meniscal tears, which may be traumatic or degenerative, disrupt the joint’s shock absorption and mechanics, producing pain, locking, and functional limitation. Cartilage loss, joint effusion, synovitis, bone contusions, fractures, and Baker (popliteal) cysts are additional findings that cause symptoms and influence management.

MRI is central to evaluating the knee because it depicts all of these structures, including ligaments, menisci, articular cartilage, and bone, without ionizing radiation, providing a comprehensive whole-joint assessment that other modalities cannot match. However, MRI interpretation varies across readers and practice settings, and access to subspecialty-trained musculoskeletal (MSK) radiologists is limited in many parts of the world. Reliable, consistent automated detection of knee abnormalities could help extend expert-level interpretation, reduce variability, and support more timely care.

The goal of this competition is to develop machine learning models that detect twelve clinically important knee abnormalities, learning from a large international dataset of knee MRI examinations paired with their original, multilingual radiology reports.

## Anatomical Overview

The knee is a synovial hinge joint formed by three bones: the femur (thigh bone) above, the tibia (shin bone) below, and the patella (kneecap) in front. The ends of these bones are covered by articular cartilage, a smooth layer that allows near-frictionless motion and distributes load. The joint is enclosed by a capsule lined with synovium, which produces lubricating fluid; an abnormal excess of this fluid is termed a joint effusion, and inflammation of the synovium is termed synovitis.

![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F413040%2Fe6095eef091115d6f20f3d5c071dd72e%2Fimage1.jpg?generation=1786032010214772&alt=media)

![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F413040%2Fc6429a733527b6dd080a84a472a6a34c%2Fimage2.jpg?generation=1786032025815728&alt=media)

*Knee anatomy: anterior view (top) and lateral view (bottom), showing the femur, tibia, patella, cruciate ligaments, and meniscus. Illustrations by BruceBlaus, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

For the purposes of this challenge, the knee is considered in three compartments. The medial compartment lies between the medial femoral condyle and the medial tibial plateau, on the inner side of the knee. The lateral compartment lies between the lateral femoral condyle and the lateral tibial plateau, on the outer side. The patellofemoral compartment lies between the patella and the femoral trochlea, the groove on the front of the femur. Osteoarthritis, or cartilage loss, is assessed separately in each of these three compartments.

Four ligaments stabilize the knee. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) lie within the joint, in the intercondylar notch, and control front-to-back stability and rotation. The medial collateral ligament (MCL) and lateral collateral ligament (LCL) run along the inner and outer sides of the knee and resist side-to-side stress. This challenge focuses on tears of the ACL and the MCL.

Between the femur and tibia sit two menisci, the medial meniscus and the lateral meniscus, C-shaped wedges of fibrocartilage that cushion the joint, absorb shock, and improve the fit between the rounded femur and the relatively flat tibia. Tears of the medial and lateral meniscus are evaluated separately.

Other relevant structures include the bone marrow within the femur, tibia, and patella, where a bruise from impact is called a bone contusion (or bone marrow edema) and a break in the bone is a fracture; and the soft tissues behind the knee, where a fluid-filled outpouching of the joint lining is called a Baker, or popliteal, cyst.

## Imaging Overview

Several modalities can image the knee. Radiographs (X-rays) show bones and joint-space narrowing but cannot directly visualize ligaments, menisci, or cartilage. Ultrasound and CT have specific roles but offer limited soft-tissue contrast for the internal structures of the joint. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the reference standard for evaluating internal derangement of the knee because it provides excellent soft-tissue contrast, depicts ligaments, menisci, cartilage, and bone marrow simultaneously, and does not use ionizing radiation.

A knee MRI examination is not a single image but a set of series, each acquired with a particular pulse sequence and in a particular imaging plane. The three standard planes are axial (cross-sectional, viewed as if looking up through the leg), coronal (a front-facing, side-to-side view), and sagittal (a side-profile, front-to-back view). Different structures are best seen in different planes; for example, the cruciate ligaments and menisci are well evaluated on sagittal and coronal images, and the patellofemoral cartilage on axial images.

Sequences differ in how they weight tissue signal. Fluid-sensitive sequences, such as proton-density or T2-weighted images, often with fat suppression, make edema, effusion, and tears appear bright and are central to detecting most abnormalities; a meniscal tear, for instance, appears as abnormally increased signal that reaches the surface of the meniscus on more than one image. Other sequences emphasize anatomy or cartilage detail. Interpreting a study therefore requires integrating information across multiple series, planes, and slices for the same knee, an inherently three-dimensional task.

![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F413040%2F055d8dc92fe53e98325b81b9eae26dee%2Fimage3.jpg?generation=1786032046408361&alt=media)

*Sagittal proton-density, fat-suppressed (fluid-sensitive) MRI of the knee, the type of sequence on which most abnormalities are detected. Image by Ptrump16, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

For the purpose of the 2026 Knee Abnormality Challenge, a “fluid sensitive” sequence refers to one in which edema, hemorrhage, and other types of fluid appear bright and fat is suppressed in some way.

Because findings can be subtle and the criteria for what counts as clinically significant are nuanced, interpretation varies between readers. This variability, combined with limited access to subspecialty MSK radiologists, motivates the development of consistent automated tools.

## Label Description

Models are evaluated on twelve binary labels, each indicating the presence or absence of a specific finding in the imaged knee. The labels, and the criteria used by the annotating radiologists, are summarized below. In each case, ambiguous or borderline findings (“on the fence”) were graded as negative to favor specificity.

ACL tear: A high-grade partial or full-thickness tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, meaning complete discontinuity of the ligament, or more than 50 percent of fibers disrupted, with or without secondary signs such as characteristic pivot-shift bone contusions. Mild signal change, degeneration, or thickening without discontinuity is graded negative.

MCL tear: A high-grade partial or complete acute tear of the medial collateral ligament, with disrupted fibers and edema within and adjacent to the ligament. Low-grade sprains and chronic or remote stress changes are graded negative.

Medial meniscus tear: Abnormal signal that definitely contacts the meniscal surface on at least two images, or a morphologic abnormality such as a truncated, diminutive, or displaced fragment, involving the medial meniscus. Intrasubstance degeneration that does not reach the surface is negative.

Lateral meniscus tear: The same criteria applied to the lateral meniscus.

Medial compartment osteoarthritis: A moderate or large area (roughly 1 cm or greater) of high-grade cartilage loss, defined as greater than 50 percent of cartilage thickness, in the medial compartment, with or without underlying subchondral marrow changes.

Lateral compartment osteoarthritis: The same criteria applied to the lateral compartment.

Patellofemoral compartment osteoarthritis: The same criteria applied to the patellofemoral compartment.

Joint effusion: A moderate or large amount of fluid distending the joint.

Synovitis: Inflammation and thickening of the synovial lining of the joint.

Baker (popliteal) cyst: A moderate or large fluid collection in the characteristic location behind the knee.

Contusion: A bone contusion, seen as bone marrow edema-like signal from impact, without a discrete fracture line.

Acute fracture: An acute cortical break or fracture line.

Each study in the annotated reference set was independently labeled by two subspecialty-trained MSK radiologists, with disagreements adjudicated by a third radiologist to produce a single consensus ground truth. Labels are assigned at the level of the whole examination, for a single knee.

The following annotated examples, drawn from the challenge’s image annotation guidelines, illustrate representative positive and negative cases for several of the labels. In each figure, yellow arrows and arrowheads mark the findings described in the caption.

title: How to get started + Competition's Official Discord

messages.text:
### Information for newbies
**New to machine learning and data science?** No question is too basic or too simple. Feel free to start your own thread, or use this thread as a place to post any first-timer clarifying questions for the Kaggle community to help you with!

**New to Kaggle?** Take a look at a few videos to learn a bit more about [site etiquette](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aIus8si_Et0), [Kaggle lingo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sEJHyuWKd-s), and [how to enter a competition using Kaggle Notebooks](https://www.youtube.com/watch?&v=GJBOMWpLpTQ). Publish and share your [models on Kaggle Models](https://www.kaggle.com/docs/models#publishing-a-model)!

**Looking for a team?** Express your interest in joining a team through our [Team Up](https://www.kaggle.com/discussions/product-feedback/341195) feature.

**Remember**: Kaggle is for everyone. Whether you're teaming up or sharing tips in the competition forum, we expect everyone to follow our Kaggle community guidelines.

### Competition's Official Discord
In addition to this competition forum, you can continue the discussion in our official Kaggle Discord Server here:
# [discord.gg/kaggle](http://discord.gg/kaggle)
 
The Discord is a great place to ask getting started questions, chat about the nuances of this competition, and connect with potential team mates. Learn more about Discord at our [announcement here](https://www.kaggle.com/discussions/general/429933). Here are a few things to keep in mind though:

**1. Discord Competition Channels are 'Public' - Don't Share Private Information**

Discord channels for specific competitions are considered 'public' spaces where you are allowed to talk about competition details. Please remember that private sharing of competition code or data outside of your team is, as always, not permitted. Code sharing must always be done publicly through the Kaggle forums/notebooks.

**2. Discord Competition Channels are Not Monitored by Staff - Keep Important Information on the Kaggle Forums**

Kaggle Staff and Hosts running competitions will not monitor Discord or be available to answer questions in Discord. This is intended to be a more casual space to discuss competitions and help each other. Please keep important questions, insights, writeups, and other valuable conversation on the Kaggle forums. 

Happy modeling!

Looking forward to experimenting with different approaches, following the discussions, and improving my skills throughout the competition. Best of luck to everyone participating!

title: Use of Commercially Hosted LLMs

messages.text:
Thanks for the clarification! Just one quick question: if LLM-generated labels/embeddings from the reports are allowed, would it also be okay to use an external LLM to extract structured features like findings, laterality, or severity and combine those with MRI features?

And would this be allowed at inference time only if those same features can be generated from the information available at inference?

Use of commercially hosted LLMs and other external inference services is permitted, provided that the service and method of use otherwise comply with the Competition Rules, including requirements that external data, models, software, and associated tools be reasonably accessible to all participants and of minimal cost. 

In other words, for purposes of this competition, submitting Competition Data, including report text, to an external LLM or API for inference or other computational processing (for example, extracting labels from reports) will not, by itself, be considered prohibited **PRIVATE SHARING** of Competition Data outside the Team.

Please refer to the [RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection Competition Rules](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/rules).  This is in accordance to Section 2.6.b, **EXTERNAL DATA AND TOOLS**.

The **PRIVATE SHARING** restriction is intended to prohibit sharing Competition Data, code, or competition-specific work product with other participants, teams, or third parties for collaboration or competitive use outside the registered Team.

Participants remain responsible for ensuring that any external service complies with all applicable Competition Rules and the service's terms of use, including the requirements for reasonable accessibility and minimal cost.

The Competition Host reserves the right to determine whether a particular service, model, or configuration is reasonably accessible, is prohibitively costly, or otherwise creates an unfair competitive advantage.

I know that the answer may be abvious but i just want to make 100% sure i can save me so much trouble and focus on model not in getting the target labels without been kicked out from the competence.
Thanks!
You can use LLM API, such as those from OpenAI, to read the reports to generate the labels.

To make the dataset question above concrete: the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) is free of charge and open to any researcher after a click-through data use agreement, but the agreement limits use to non-commercial research. The same access pattern covers MRNet, fastMRI+ and SKM-TEA, so a ruling on the category would settle it for essentially every public knee-MRI resource. Given the prize money, could the host confirm whether external datasets under research-only agreements are permitted, and if so whether the winners' open-source obligation is affected? Teams need this before committing pretraining work ahead of the entry deadline. Thank you.

From the competition’s perspective, use of these datasets would be considered non-commercial; receipt of competition prize money does not, by itself, make their use a commercial sale or commercial exploitation. These datasets would not be excluded by the competition rules solely because their licenses restrict use to non-commercial purposes.

A separate consideration is whether an external dataset is reasonably accessible to all competitors. Datasets that can be accessed through a straightforward registration or click-through data-use agreement would generally satisfy this requirement. By contrast, datasets requiring institution-specific approvals, negotiated written agreements, IRB approval, lengthy credentialing, or other substantial administrative steps may present a meaningful accessibility barrier, particularly given the remaining competition timeline. Such requirements could therefore affect whether a dataset is considered allowable under the competition’s external-data rules, independent of whether its use is characterized as commercial or non-commercial.

Our job (Host) is tough here because RSNA and Kaggle do not own or control these external datasets and cannot interpret or waive their individual data-use agreements, expedite requests and so on, on behalf of the dataset owners. Teams remain responsible for ensuring that their intended use, including participation in a prize-bearing competition and any required release of code or models, is permitted under the applicable dataset license or agreement.

Therefore, to the extent the question concerns the *competition rules*, readily accessible datasets with non-commercial restrictions are not prohibited on that basis alone. Dataset-specific licensing obligations remain the responsibility of each team, and datasets involving substantial approval or access hurdles may need to be considered separately under the competition’s equal-accessibility requirements.

Sorry for the verbose response. I hope it's at least a little helpful...

This is a very welcome clarification from the organizers. Allowing the use of commercially hosted LLMs (like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google APIs) for tasks like text parsing, label extraction, or metadata enrichment really opens up creative pipeline designs especially for handling the report text efficiently.It’s great to see the rules explicitly state that API inference doesn't count as prohibited private sharing, provided the tools remain lowcost and accessible to everyone. It gives teams the green light to leverage state-of-the-art text processing without the fear of accidental disqualification. Thanks for highlighting this section!

Any commercial use, sale, or **other monetization is prohibited**."

The rules about commercially hosted LLMs are important here. Since knee MRI interpretation requires domain expertise, it's tempting to use an LLM to help with reasoning. But the competition rules likely restrict this to ensure the solutions are based on the image data, not external reasoning. Check the rules page carefully before incorporating any LLM-based features.

title: Welcome to Knee Abnormality Detection Challenge!

messages.text:
The knee is the largest joint in the human body, and MRI is central to diagnosing major sports injuries, trauma, and degenerative disease, but interpretation is demanding and access to subspecialty musculoskeletal expertise is uneven. 

This challenge invites the RSNA and Kaggle community to build models that detect 12 clinically important knee abnormalities, spanning ligament and meniscal tears, osteoarthritis, effusion, synovitis, fracture, and more.

This is also RSNA’s first AI Challenge to pair MRI examinations with original multilingual radiology reports. We hope that combination encourages creative, rigorous work that reflects the **real **clinical task: connecting images, language, and meaningful patient care.

And don't forget the efficiency prizes!   "Real world" here also means striking a balance between label-level accuracy and efficient use of resources.

A challenge dataset can make a large collaborative effort look deceptively simple. We are deeply grateful to the contributing institutions, radiologists, data and privacy teams, RSNA colleagues, and Kaggle team who made this possible.  

Above all, we owe it to you... every participant who will bring curiosity, technical skill, and healthy skepticism to the work. Whether this is your first Kaggle competition or your hundredth, we hope you will share reproducible ideas, learn from one another, and help move imaging AI forward thoughtfully. 

Good luck, and welcome.

Learn more about the challenge and [RSNA’s AI Challenge program](https://www.rsna.org/artificial-intelligence/ai-image-challenge).

先看失败的那次提交日志里第一条 traceback，而不是只看编辑器中交互运行的结果。提交会从保存的版本在干净环境重跑；草稿会话里已有的变量或临时文件，不能当作提交时一定存在。

我在这个比赛复现 Notebook 时会依次查：① Input 是否附上比赛数据和所有模型权重；比赛数据可能挂在 /kaggle/input/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection，也可能是 /kaggle/input/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection，先用 Path.exists() 确认；② 保存版本后从头 Run All 是否成功；③ 日志是否显示 GPU/内存不足或依赖安装失败；④ 最终 submission 文件是否按要求生成。

如果方便，贴出失败版本日志中最早的异常类型和附近几行（隐去个人信息/密钥），才能判断这次到底是哪一步失败。单凭 ‘Notebook Threw Exception’ 无法确定原因。
run all是正常可以的logs中也是successfully，只是在提交运行后一两小时的时候直接Threw Exception，在保存运行是成功的

title: Kaggle could we please start doing something about the public notebooks?

messages.text:
There's a reason your post has received so many upvotes. You're pointing out the elephant in the room.

I've never really understood the point of sharing notebooks that anyone can simply copy and submit for a high leaderboard score when a competition is nearing its end. I'm aware of Kaggle's restriction on publishing new notebooks during the final week (although there are ways around it), but I don't think a week is always a realistic amount of time for participants to learn from these solutions and meaningfully build on them. It also makes it disproportionately important to keep a close eye on the competition during that final week, potentially outweighing weeks of work leading up to it.

There's something a bit shady about the incentives behind it, whichever way you look at it:

(a) If your notebook is overfitted to the public leaderboard (as often happens), you're potentially misleading other participants and sending them down the wrong path.

(b) If it actually generalizes, you've effectively raised the bar overnight. People who've spent weeks developing their own solutions can suddenly find themselves pushed out of medal range by a flood of copied submissions.

So whether (a) or (b) turns out to be true, some participants end up paying the price. Notebook medals are supposed to reward contributions that help the community learn, yet the current system incentivizes a practice that can come at the expense of that very same community. That seems to defeat the purpose of rewarding notebook sharing in the first place.

I think this gets even worse in the newer agent competitions. If a public agent gets copied over and over, the opponent pool can become saturated with identical strategies. That can encourage people to optimize specifically against whatever happens to be overrepresented on the ladder, rather than developing agents that perform well against a wider range of opponents. Depending on the nature of the competition and how matchmaking works, this can produce some pretty misleading signals about what actually works.

Of course, experienced competitors will generally know how to recognize signs of overfitting and test how well a solution generalizes. But for less experienced participants, this adds a lot of unnecessary noise and confusion.

And don't get me wrong. I'm all for discussions, working notes, and people sharing experiments and what they've learned. I've personally learned far more from discussion posts that offered a few hints and opened up directions I hadn't even considered than from notebooks I could simply copy and submit. I just think the current system needs some rethinking if we want a healthier competitive environment. 

Paradoxically, public notebooks might lower the barrier to entry, but end up raising the bar for newcomers trying to compete with their own work. Making it easier to copy a strong solution doesn't necessarily make a competition more accessible to those who actually want to learn and develop their own solutions. And that's something Kaggle should take seriously.

Hi @cody11null,

Thank you for sharing your concerns. Seeing low-effort notebooks getting rewarded is indeed frustrating and not something that we want either. We have spent considerable time internally discussing this.

Unfortunately, it's been difficult to come up with a policy that's able to discriminate reliably between low-effort copying or blending and something that meaningfully builds off of the ideas of others. You're right too that the system incentivizes marginal (and often meaningless) improvements to the public leaderboard, because the public leaderboard score is often seen (erroneously) as the best judge of the quality of a notebook. You might take consolation in knowing that low-effort ensembles like this usually suffer from optimism bias from overfitting and tend to drop on the private leaderboard (perhaps because the score is just from a lucky random seed, as you pointed out).

We do though still have a notebook publishing lock (one week, in this competition) before the submission deadline. And please do report verbatim copies with scrubbed attribution so we can act on them; whatever the case, people should be getting credit for their work. Use **Report** on the notebook and link the original.

Respectfully, I believe there are several ways to address this issue, depending on which approach Kaggle would prefer to take. Below are two relatively low-impact ideas that have been brought up in previous discussions and would allow the community to help address the problem natrually.

1. Separating forks from upvotes again - So that notebooks that are quickly copied and submitted aren't so rewarded, only truly thoughtful work would be. 

2. Adding a downvote option - So that the community can start punishing these low effort notebooks on our own. 

Yes, there is an existing delay preventing new public notebooks with 7 days (which to me personally to me seems too tight, though I know there is reasonable debate), but this system doesnt handle updating existing notebooks which was a massive problem in the last several competitions I have been in. Even competitions without that public LB bias like the last santa competition had high placing code being shared less than an hour before competition end.

These are just a couple of relatively simple ideas, and I'm sure there are trade-offs to consider with each. The underlying problem, however, is that the current incentives can reward the rapid redistribution of existing solutions over original experimentation, meaningful discussion, and learning.

Kaggle is home to some of the brightest minds in the world, both among its competitors and its administrators. Surely, we can find a fair solution that preserves open collaboration while better rewarding genuine contributions to the community.

I do also greatly appreciate your response!
can we link the low effort notebook to the original notebook so the author get the credits (upvotes)?
What if 1 low effort notebook is linked to another low effort notebook @konohayui?

To be honest, over the past few days, I’ve seen a lot of discussion about fairness around competition data and code analysis in the discussion forums. I’ve even seen people ask why the top 10 can achieve such high scores when they can’t, and suggest that it’s unfair unless those competitors explain how they did it.
First, we’re taking part in a competition. Differences in performance and rankings are part of what a competition is about, especially when prestigious recognition and prize money are at stake.
Second, having such an open, supportive culture of sharing within a competitive environment is genuinely rare. Take the notebooks I’ve shared, for example: every new model and every new set of weights has cost me considerable time, effort, and money, including server and compute costs. A large part of why I’m willing to share them for free is that I hope my contributions can help everyone achieve better scores. I also hope to earn recognition for my work and perhaps become a Notebooks Grandmaster one day. Without incentives like these, I can easily imagine the quality of community contributions declining.
That’s why I don’t think there’s anything fundamentally wrong with the system the Kaggle team has designed. If you’ve spent a lot of time on other similar forums, you’ll find that Kaggle is one of the best communities out there.
Even so, after I updated one of my datasets and some people could no longer reproduce the score with one click, I was accused of misleading people to get upvotes.
Of course, I understand that any community will have different perspectives and opinions. I’ll continue putting in the work to achieve better results and sharing those results publicly with everyone. I wish everyone in the community and the Kaggle team all the best.

Yet again, we have another competition where low-effort public ensembles are being released with less than two weeks remaining, potentially allowing participants to secure medals through copy-paste submissions rather than their own work or understanding.

I fully expect this to continue as the deadline approaches and based on the past year or more, I expect that Kaggle will do absolutely nothing to address it.

Personally, I expect to be fine. My concern is for the participants who may end up hundreds of places below where they otherwise would have finished, despite putting in significantly more work and developing their own solutions. I am equally concerned about those who have shared genuinely valuable notebooks and helped others learn, only to see that work receive little recognition because the current code-tier structure disproportionately rewards marginal leaderboard improvements, often effectively meaningless (or outright duplicates), driven by a random seed rather than a meaningful contribution.

What I find most frustrating is not simply that this problem persists, but that it continues despite repeated forum discussions and substantial community support highlighting the issue. **Why have we received so little meaningful explanation from Kaggle about why this remains unresolved, what trade-offs are preventing a solution, or whether there is any concrete plan to address it?**

No system will be perfect, and I recognize that solutions involve trade-offs. But leaving participants without meaningful explanation while the same concerns recur competition after competition is difficult to justify.

Kaggle should be a place where competitive performance, original work, and meaningful contributions are rewarded. Right now, the incentives are increasingly misaligned with those goals, and I would genuinely like to understand why.

title: Reaching 0.949 with one CoAtNet: labels, native crops, and anatomical mirroring

messages.text:
Our best single-model submission scores **0.949 public AUC**. We are sharing the accuracy recipe, our smaller 0.945 model for the efficiency track, and several changes that did not help.

The accuracy result uses one CoAtNet checkpoint trained at 384 pixels. At inference we take a native 320-pixel center crop and average probabilities from the original view and an anatomical left/right mirror. It is one learned model evaluated twice. The checkpoint itself averages three selected epochs from one training run, called SWA in our code.

## The score history

These are ordinary, full twelve-finding public leaderboard scores. Rows describe successive pipeline configurations; their differences are not all isolated causal effects.

| Configuration | Public AUC | Change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Our all-data CoAtNet, 80 slices and 78 windows | 0.939 | Starting point |
| 96 slices, native 384-pixel cache, 94 windows | 0.940 | +0.001 |
| Blend + JEV labels | 0.942 | +0.002 |
| Smaller 224-pixel crop model with epoch weight averaging | 0.940 | −0.002 |
| Add external OAI knee examples with masked labels | 0.945 | +0.005 |
| 384-pixel, full-field external-data recipe | 0.948 | +0.003 |
| Same weights, native 320-pixel inference crop | 0.948 | 0.000 |
| Same weights and crop, anatomical mirror probability averaging | **0.949** | **+0.001** |

The first density change also changed cached resolution and window count. Adding external examples increased training rows and optimizer updates, and the serving precision path changed. The 224-to-384 step also changed training crop geometry and the pretrained architecture variant. Those rows should be read as recipe comparisons rather than additive gains from individual factors.

## Training and labels

The model is a timm CoAtNet backbone with finding-specific multiple-instance attention pooling. We trained on 4,349 report-labeled competition studies; the 58 expert-labeled studies were excluded from training but reused for selection. The weak targets combine our report-derived soft labels with the public label sources credited below. In the external-data recipe, 2,399 OAI knees brought the training set to 6,748 rows. PF OA, Lateral OA and Synovitis received external supervision; unavailable finding cells were masked rather than treated as negatives. Positive class weights remained based on RSNA labels.

Both released candidates use seed 42, 16 epochs, backbone learning rate 4.01e−5, head learning rate 0.00195 and weight decay 0.0588. Training used 12 windows per study, batch size 1 and gradient accumulation over 16 studies; gold evaluation used 24 windows. The smaller model averages epochs 15, 13 and 12; the accuracy model averages epochs 14, 11 and 12. These selected averages are called SWA in our code. Adding external examples increased the scheduled optimizer updates from 4,336 to 6,736, so that comparison is not compute-matched.

## The final inference recipe

Each study has 96 preprocessed slices across five sagittal, coronal, and axial series slots. We evaluate 94 three-slice windows, process them in chunks of 16, and use finding-specific attention over the complete window bag.

For the accuracy model, native 384×384 windows are cropped to pixels `[32:352, 32:352]`. No resize is applied. Sagittal left/right mirroring reverses the three slice channels; coronal and axial mirroring flips image width. We use the center slice to determine the window plane and apply the transform before normalization. We average the two sigmoid probability vectors equally. The existing final per-finding percentile ranking preserves their ordering.

The smaller model uses a 307-pixel center crop resized to 224 pixels, the same 94-window policy, FP16 autocast, and one view. It scores 0.945. Recorded submit-to-score turnaround was about 7.2 minutes for that entry and 26.1 minutes for the mirrored accuracy entry. These include queueing and orchestration; they are **not official inference runtimes or efficiency ranks**.

## What did not help

| Tested change | Public AUC, reference → result |
|---|---:|
| Older model: 94 windows reduced to 24 | 0.940 → 0.934 |
| Older model: width-flip TTA across every imaging plane | 0.940 → 0.939 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 304 pixels | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Current weights: native crop reduced from 320 to 288 pixels | 0.948 → 0.946 |
| Epoch 14 instead of averaged weights, same 320-pixel inference | 0.948 → 0.947 |
| Fresh training with corrected batch-normalization checkpoint replay | 0.948 → 0.944 |
| Fresh native 320-pixel crop training, anatomical mirror inference | 0.949 → 0.946 |

The all-plane width flip is different from anatomical mirroring, and it was tested on an older checkpoint. Its failure does not establish a controlled comparison between the mirror implementations. The new crop-trained model also failed to replace the incumbent despite encouraging gold diagnostics.

Our 58 labeled studies were reused for checkpoint selection and development. They are useful diagnostics, not independent cross-validation. For example, epoch 14 improved gold AUC while losing on the public board. Rounded public-score differences, especially +0.001, do not establish statistical significance or a private-test gain.

## Credits and release references

Thanks to [dreaddevelopment for the public Raptor CoAtNet/MIL recipe and baseline weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dreaddevelopment/raptor-knee-widedense). That public checkpoint scored 0.924 in our baseline read; it is context, rather than a controlled starting point for the table. Our selected checkpoints were retrained. The public weak-label contributions include [stevenleehans](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stevenleehans/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels), [pilkwang](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels), and [riadmohamed42's JEV labels and verification](https://www.kaggle.com/code/riadmohamed42/jev-knee-labels-verification). We thank RSNA and the competition data contributors.

Reproducibility notebooks: [accuracy, 0.949](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0949-anatomical-mirror) and [efficiency, 0.945](https://www.kaggle.com/code/nartaa/rsna-knee-0945-efficient-224crop). The [selected learned weights](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nartaa/rsna-knee-publication-swa-weights-20261007) are a separate minimal dependency. Both notebooks preserve the exact scored scientific inference source and checkpoint hashes, include hardware/environment requirements, and are saved statically without running inference. No OAI images, identifiers, records, raw reports, subject-level labels or predictions are distributed.

Both models used the same 2,399 baseline OAI knees; the unsuccessful 12-month arm is excluded from these release models. The public Study describes aggregate methods/results while its exact-input linkage manifest remains restricted to qualified researchers.

Data and/or research tools used in the preparation of this manuscript were obtained and analyzed from the controlled access datasets distributed from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI), a data repository housed within the NIMH Data Archive (NDA). OAI is a collaborative informatics system created by the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute of Arthritis, Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) to provide a worldwide resource to quicken the pace of biomarker identification, scientific investigation and OA drug development. Dataset identifier(s): 10.15154/0hcg-f676.

[Shared NDA Study](https://nda.nih.gov/study.html?id=3407) · [DOI: 10.15154/0hcg-f676](https://doi.org/10.15154/0hcg-f676). Official acknowledgement source: [NDA manuscript preparation](https://nda.nih.gov/nda/manuscript-preparation).

title: Local CV or Public LB: which one can we trust?

messages.text:
In this competition, the only expert-labelled data available for local validation are the 58 gold training studies. That makes local validation unusually challenging.

I compared two local validation scores against the public LB across 15 of my own submissions, each based on five-fold CV:

![](https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F3858775%2Fa49d8034870b2413899e6f01816b9ba9%2F2026-10-10%2017.32.37.png?generation=1791621169971924&alt=media)

* AUC on the 58 gold studies vs. public LB: r = 0.66.
* AUC on ~4,300 studies with LLM-extracted labels vs. public LB: r = 0.87.

For my submissions, higher CV scores on the LLM-extracted (weak) labels have generally gone hand in hand with higher public LB scores. AUC on the 58 gold studies tracked the public LB less closely.

My current thinking:

* The public LB uses ~30% of the test set, which is much larger than 58 studies. It may therefore provide a more reliable signal, though sample size alone doesn't guarantee that.
* For local validation, evaluating out-of-fold predictions against the LLM-extracted labels across the training set might be the most practical option after all.

I'd love to hear how others are approaching validation here, and whether you've seen similar patterns. I'm also curious how much of a leaderboard shake-up people expect at the end.

Slightly off-topic, but since the metric is AUC: submitting 1 − p instead of p gives you 1 − AUC on the public LB. Because the leaderboard only displays each team's best score, a team could use this to track improvements without revealing its actual performance, then flip the predictions back at the end.

So there may be some strong teams flying under the radar. It'll be interesting to watch the LB in the final days.

title: Clarification on eligibility of OAI dataset

messages.text:
In [this topic thread](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/741819) it was stated that ` OAI is fine as long as it's "generally accessible to all participants" without institutional sign-off and free of charge`.

But several people in [this topic thread](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/746792) say they can't register at all from China.

There is also an [NDA notice](https://nda.nih.gov/nda/enhancing-dar-security-measures) which clearly states that since Aprlil 4 2025, NIH prohibits access to "NDA data by researchers and institutions located in countries of concern, including China (including Hong Kong and Macau), Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, and Venezuela".

OAI is hosted on NDA.

China isn't on the competition's excluded list (Rule 3.1), and Rule 2.6.b mentions "geo restrictions" as something that can make external data not "reasonably accessible to all". That sounds a lot like the uneven-access reason KneeCoT was ruled out for in [this topic thread](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/734109)

Is OAI allowed, given that participants in some eligible countries can't access it?

title: Optimizations for blazingly fast submissions (<10 minutes!) + Looking for teammates :)

messages.text:
Solo, 0.949 public (that is nartaa's public notebook run as is, no credit claimed). Looking to team up before Oct 15.

What I can bring:
- LLM-read labels for all 4,407 training reports (12 findings, three independent reads, stored as probabilities), plus an honest A/B on held-out gold: the triple-read labels did NOT beat a simpler single-read mix. Useful negative result, happy to share.
- A 5-fold CoAtNet-2 384 leg: 0.935 public alone, 0.948 in a rank blend with the public 0.949. Weights and OOF predictions ready to share.
- Careful bookkeeping: one change per submission, a registry with gold-set deltas and bootstrap CIs.
- Background: credit-risk modelling lead, comfortable with validation design and calibration. Small GPU budget.

Looking for someone with a stronger single model or a different backbone/view strategy who wants a careful validation partner. DM or reply here.

On inference, I went from ~40 min to under 10 with a CoAtNet. A few things that helped, which might transfer:

- One model copy per GPU, each with its own shard of studies - replacing DataParallel, which re-broadcasts every parameter on each forward call. 
- Read each DICOM once, concurrently. One threaded pass per series serves both slice ordering and pixels. A single reader gets ~59 MB/s from /kaggle/input; 16 threads get ~372.
- Parse DICOM headers directly instead of through pydicom: 0.307 → 0.058 ms/file.
- Read pixels straight from the PixelData offset (np.frombuffer) - bit-identical to pydicom, 1.22 → 0.33 ms/slice.
- Take the 1st/99th percentiles on a strided subsample. np.percentile sorts, and that sort was ~60% of decode time.
- fp16 weights with half inputs, no autocast - 2.08× over autocast on a T4.
- uint8 to the GPU, normalise on device, pinned memory, non-blocking copies, persistent workers.

***Looking for teammates strong on labels/targets or bringing a resilient single model submission > 0.940.***

title: EDA: labels, co-occurrence and MRI views (official data only)

messages.text:
Hi all,

I put together an EDA notebook for this competition that might help anyone getting started: https://www.kaggle.com/code/eeshsaxena/rsna-knee-eda-labels-and-mri-views

A few things that stood out to me:

Only 58 training studies come with labels. Effusion is the most common finding (about 60%) and MCL the rarest (about 16%). With so few studies the 95% intervals span roughly 20 to 25 percentage points, so local validation will be noisy.
None of the labelled studies is completely normal. A study has about four positive findings on average, and 54 of the 58 studies have a label combination of their own, so there is no small set of typical patterns.
The data is big and varied: 24,371 series and about 819k DICOM files, with a real mix of scanners, field strengths, slice thicknesses and planes.
The data page lists JPEG Lossless and JPEG 2000 transfer syntaxes. The files I sampled were uncompressed, but the default Kaggle image cannot decode the compressed ones without pylibjpeg or gdcm, so it is worth guarding for that in a submission notebook.

It runs on CPU in about two minutes and uses only the official files. If you spot anything wrong or want another plot added, let me know in the comments.

title: External data behind an institutional data use agreement - does the KneeCoT ruling generalize?

messages.text:
Thanks to the host for the clear ruling on KneeCoT (topic 734109). The stated reasoning was that a dataset requiring a formal data agreement with the providing institution can make the playing field uneven.

Could the host confirm whether that interpretation generalizes to other knee MRI datasets that are free of charge but gated behind an institutional agreement - for example OAI (NIH/NIMH Data Archive), which requires a signed Data Use Certification from an institution holding an active Federal Wide Assurance, or MRNet (Stanford), which requires a Research Use Agreement.

A related question, since it bears on the same decision: winners' obligations require delivering model weights as a public Kaggle dataset, and sharing the final model publicly for open distribution and validation. If a pretrained model were derived from data under such an agreement, would publishing those weights satisfy that obligation - or does that requirement independently rule out pretraining on agreement-gated data, regardless of the license?

Asking before investing compute, so the answer is on record for everyone.

NC licenses are allowed from the host's perspective,[ as mentioned here](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/733965#3517696). ND licenses are a problem. Most external datasets that are relevant here are ND, and training a model on images, then releasing those weights as required by Kaggle winning solutions, would be a derivative and hence prohibited.

MRNet, KneeMRI, etc. all carry a ND license and I would be surpised if they are allowed for model training.
Yeah I haven’t tried any external data for this reason, would be curious if top teams are using it

Following up on the KneeCoT ruling above, and on your note in "Use of Commercially Hosted LLMs" distinguishing "straightforward registration or click-through" access from "institution-specific approvals, negotiated written agreements, IRB approval, lengthy credentialing" -- could you confirm which side of that line these fall on:

- MRNet (Stanford AIMI): a Research Use Agreement accepted via click-through on the AIMI portal
- fastMRI (NYU, raw k-space/DICOM release): requires emailing NYU and waiting on an approved data-sharing agreement
- OAI (NIH-funded, accessed via a federal data archive): requires a signed Data Use Certification
- SKM-TEA (Stanford AIMI): same access pattern as MRNet

A ruling per access-pattern (click-through vs. emailed/signed agreement) rather than per dataset would help everyone here, since most of the open questions on this board reduce to the same two patterns. Thanks for the KneeCoT ruling above -- trying to apply it correctly before committing pretraining compute.
Not sure if external data is permitted—but if I do training or label cleaning locally, it's unlikely anyone would be able to tell. Definitely something to think about.

Sure, but the competition rules state that your published results have to be replicable. This isn't possible if you don't disclose all of your training data. I suppose it doesn't matter if you're not trying to win, but in that case, why bother?

A related edge case I would appreciate clarification on:

Suppose a pretrained model checkpoint is publicly downloadable, free of charge, and equally accessible to every competition participant, but the authors originally pretrained it partly on a private clinical cohort that competition participants themselves cannot access.

Participants would use only the public pretrained checkpoint, not the underlying private data.

Would that public checkpoint be considered an acceptable external model under the competition’s “reasonably accessible to all” rule?

I am specifically trying to distinguish this case from directly using an external dataset that requires a DUA or institutional access. The resource actually used by competitors would be the freely available pretrained model, while some of its historical pretraining data would not itself be reproducible or accessible.

A host ruling would be helpful before deciding whether such a model can be included in a final solution.

Lets take your thought a tiny bit further.  I don't have access to any of the data used to train ChatGPT, Gemini Pro, or Claude.
For that matter Dino V2 training data is hidden from me.

What do you think the host would say about the use of these models?

Think the answer given in another post - its our job to understand the restrictions of any data or model used.

I myself not worried about this particular rule.  It only comes into play if you are a winner.  

I see no way in heck I am going to make it to the top 10 - this (IMO) is a really hard set of data and matching what the radiologists reported based on only 58 gold images is a shake up in the making.

I got  7 day ban from discussion a few months ago for suggesting to someone pretty new that the probability of winning was approaching 0.0.

@javaduke95 Could you please provide an official host ruling on comment #3519419? Specifically, is a freely downloadable checkpoint trained on inaccessible private clinical data allowed, and can it satisfy winner-delivery requirements when its repository only declares Apache-2.0 in the README but provides no LICENSE file or checkpoint-specific terms?

We need clarification before using MRI-CORE

title: 8 public LLM label sets vs gold-58: 11 of 12 findings show no clear difference

messages.text:
Many of us train on LLM labels read from the reports, and there are now several public sets. I scored
  eight of them on the 58 gold studies, with a 95% bootstrap CI for every source and finding
  (class-stratified, 2,000 resamples).

  Result: for 11 of 12 findings, the best and the median set are not clearly different. MCL has 9
  positives, too few to rank. On gold-74 (with JEV's 16 extra studies) all 12 findings show no clear

  A plain mean of six CC0 sets has a CI that overlaps the best single set on all 12 findings. Macro AUC on
  gold-58: consensus 0.8887, steven_v4 0.8927, steven_v2 0.8873.

  | Finding | Gold-58 positives | Verdict | Best source (AUC, 95% CI) | Consensus (AUC, 95% CI) |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | ACL | 24 | no clear difference | pilkwang 0.997 (0.988 to 1.000) | 0.993 (0.974 to 1.000) |
  | MCL | 9 | too few positives to rank sources | yunus 0.984 (0.955 to 1.000) | 0.986 (0.955 to 1.000) |
  | Medial Meniscus | 26 | no clear difference | steven_v2 0.954 (0.901 to 0.993) | 0.945 (0.885 to 0.989)
  |
  | Lateral Meniscus | 23 | no clear difference | steven_v4 0.879 (0.766 to 0.973) | 0.876 (0.759 to 0.971)
  |
  | Medial OA | 15 | no clear difference | steven_v4 0.932 (0.830 to 0.995) | 0.928 (0.811 to 0.997) |
  | Lateral OA | 11 | no clear difference | yunus 0.835 (0.662 to 0.960) | 0.818 (0.613 to 0.971) |
  | PF OA | 21 | no clear difference | steven_v4 0.902 (0.808 to 0.977) | 0.883 (0.777 to 0.972) |
  | Effusion | 35 | no clear difference | steven_v4 0.877 (0.771 to 0.955) | 0.873 (0.771 to 0.952) |
  | Synovitis | 27 | no clear difference | steven_v2 0.790 (0.670 to 0.898) | 0.751 (0.623 to 0.872) |
  | Baker's | 12 | no clear difference | steven_v2 0.946 (0.868 to 1.000) | 0.932 (0.835 to 0.998) |
  | Contusion | 19 | no clear difference | steven_v4 0.860 (0.755 to 0.942) | 0.855 (0.750 to 0.945) |
  | Fracture | 18 | no clear difference | qwen 0.876 (0.774 to 0.965) | 0.824 (0.679 to 0.942) |

  "Clear winner" would mean the best source's lower bound is above the median source's upper bound. The
  rule was set before the first gold run, with no per-finding tuning on gold.

  Limits: 58 studies is a small ruler. steven_v2's Synovitis rule was informed by gold-58, so treat
  Synovitis with care. This measures agreement with gold, not leaderboard impact.

  Consensus file (CC0) and all metrics:
  https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/karttikjangid05/rsna-knee-public-llm-label-sets-compared
, 
  Notebook: https://www.kaggle.com/code/karttikjangid05/rsna-knee-which-llm-labels-can-you-trust

  Thanks to every label author and to JEV for the 74-study set and for showing that per-finding blending on
  gold overfits.

title: [Interactive 3D Tool] Are we on the right track? Using 3D Knee Anatomy & Continuous Depth Slicing to test our ML assumptions

messages.text:
**Live Interactive 3D Simulator**: [https://www.kaggle.com/code/philgear/3d-knee-anatomy-slicing-simulator](https://www.kaggle.com/code/philgear/3d-knee-anatomy-slicing-simulator)

(Sorry for the scroll)

---

### Hi everyone,

Like many of you, we started this competition treating knee MRIs primarily as bags of 2D slices (MIL pooling, 2.5D channel stacking, multi-view convolutions). 

However, as we pushed past the ~0.93 mark, we noticed our models were occasionally treating visually similar textures as interchangeable, ignoring the fact that **an MRI scanner samples a continuous 3D physical volume**.

To test whether our anatomical intuition aligns with clinical reality, we built a **zero-dependency interactive 3D WebGL Knee Anatomy & MRI Slicing Simulator** right inside a Kaggle notebook. 

👉 **You can orbit the 3D model and scrub slice depth controls here**: [https://www.kaggle.com/code/philgear/3d-knee-anatomy-slicing-simulator](https://www.kaggle.com/code/philgear/3d-knee-anatomy-slicing-simulator)

Before we push further into this architectural direction, **we'd love to ask the community: are we on the right track with these three core hypotheses?**

---

### ❓ Question 1: Continuous Slice Depth ($z$) vs. Standard Pooling

In the 3D simulator, scrubbing the sagittal slicing plane demonstrates how deterministic anatomical landmarks are:
- $z \in [0.10, 0.25]$: Medial Meniscus (posterior & anterior horns)
- $z \in [0.42, 0.58]$: Intercondylar Notch (ACL & PCL crossing)
- $z \in [0.75, 0.90]$: Lateral Meniscus & Popliteus

When we injected continuous slice depth $z \in [0.0, 1.0]$ into a 2.5D feature extractor via a simple sinusoidal + MLP gating module (shared in the notebook), our cross-validation jumped from **0.8208 to 0.8782 Macro AUC**.

👉 **Our Question**: Are other top teams explicitly conditioning on physical slice depth (e.g., from `ImagePositionPatient` or normalized slice index), or are your 3D/MIL pooling heads learning this implicitly? Does physical depth conditioning help prevent false-positive tears in peripheral slices on your validation sets?

---

### ❓ Question 2: Laterality Canonicalization (Left vs. Right Knee Mirroring)

A subtle spatial trap we noticed when aligning coordinate frames:
- In a **Right Knee**, $z = 0.15$ is **Medial** and $z = 0.85$ is **Lateral**.
- In a **Left Knee**, $z = 0.15$ is **Lateral** and $z = 0.85$ is **Medial**!

Without laterality canonicalization, feeding a non-mirrored Left Knee into a depth-conditioned model inverts the spatial meaning of the features for roughly 50% of patients. When we canonicalized all studies to a standard Right Knee orientation (mirroring left knees based on DICOM metadata), spatial alignment snapped into place.

👉 **Our Question**: Have others found that laterality canonicalization provides a clean boost, or does standard random horizontal flip augmentation during training already make your models invariant to this?

---

### ❓ Question 3: Kinematic Triads & Biomechanical Co-Occurrence

In the simulator's findings carousel, selecting an abnormality reveals its **Companion Triad**:
- **ACL Tear** $\rightarrow$ Co-occurs with **Bone Contusion (~88%)** (pivot-shift impaction of the lateral femoral condyle against the posterior tibial plateau) and **Medial Meniscus Tear (~64%)** (O'Donoghue's Triad).
- **Baker's Cyst** $\rightarrow$ Co-occurs with **Joint Effusion (~72%)** (unidirectional fluid valve into the popliteal fossa).

We've been experimenting with **Asymmetric Loss (ASL)** ($\gamma_- = 4.0, \gamma_+ = 1.0$) and Bayesian prior smoothing to handle sparse positive findings and sharpen borderline predictions.

👉 **Our Question**: Are teams using explicit graph neural networks, Bayesian priors, or multi-task loss weightings to capture these physical dependencies? Or does standard multi-label cross-entropy already capture enough co-occurrence signal in practice?

---

### 🎨 Features in the Simulator:

If you want to test these anatomical relationships yourself in the notebook (runs 100% locally in browser, zero GPU required):
1. **Interactive Plane Slicing**: Sagittal, Coronal, and Axial planes with real-time clipping.
2. **Procedural Tissue Layers**: Toggle Bone, Musculotendinous units, and Skin envelopes.
3. **Kaizen Visual Management (*Mieruka*)**: 
   - 🔴 **Andon Red**: Acute mechanical tears (ACL, bucket-handle meniscal tears, fractures)
   - 🟡 **Kaizen Amber**: Secondary reactive effusion, bone marrow edema contusion, Baker's cysts
   - 🟢 **Kaizen Green**: Intact baseline homeostatic architecture
4. **Doctor ⟷ Patient Mode Switch**: Toggle between high-density radiological heuristics (*Blumensaat Line*, *Bow-Tie 2-Slice Rule*) and patient-facing 3-Act recovery narratives.

We'd love to hear your thoughts, feedback, and whether this matches what you're seeing in your own validation splits! 🚀
I added a game too to help teach patients, one for the waiting room.

title: Plateau at 0.903: sharing my pipeline and ablations, and looking for advice

messages.text:
Thanks to everyone’s advice, I’ve improved my public LB score to 0.935.
The suggestions helped me rethink my input pipeline, training setup, and ensembling strategy. Working through these experiments taught me a lot, and I really appreciate everyone who took the time to share their experience.
Thank you all for helping me move past that plateau!

Hi Kagglers,

My current best public score is **0.903**. I have tried several backbones and approaches to report-derived supervision, but improvements of even 0.001 are becoming difficult. Reading the [discussion about compact models reaching 0.93–0.94+ at 224/288 resolution](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/735304) has made me reconsider where to spend my next experiments.

I would appreciate advice on what to audit or ablate next. I am sharing my setup and some unsuccessful experiments so others can see what I have tried.

## Current setup

- **Labels:** report-derived soft targets for the 4,407 training studies, with masks/weights for missing, uncertain or ambiguous supervision.
- **Images:** physical slice ordering using image position projected onto the slice normal; 130-mm crops cached at 336×336; six sequence slots; 12 selected slices per available slot, mainly within the central 20–80% of the stack. Selected slices are grouped into three-channel inputs.
- **Model:** mainly DINOv2-S/14, hierarchical aggregation within and across series, and twelve learned label queries.
- **Training:** 50-epoch schedules for the DINO members, using BCE-only or BCE plus a pairwise ranking loss.
- **Validation:** five-fold CV against fixed report-derived validation targets and masks. Promising pilots are extended to the remaining folds. The 58 expert-labeled studies have already informed development, so I treat them as a development panel rather than an independent test set.

The current composition has **four model recipes, each trained on five folds: 20 checkpoints total**. Fold predictions are rank-averaged within each recipe, and the resulting family outputs are rank-normalized for composition. Each label receives three equal-weight family contributions; I have not tuned those weights.

| Role | Backbone | Model input | Epochs | Loss | Training labels |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Generalist | DINOv2-S/14 | 336 | 50 | BCE | All 12 |
| Specialist | DINOv2-S/14 | 336 | 50 | BCE | ACL, MCL, medial/lateral meniscus |
| Second DINO | DINOv2-S/14 | 336 | 50 | BCE + pairwise ranking | All 12 |
| CoAtNet | coatnet_rmlp_2_rw_384 | 384 | 25 | BCE | All 12 |

The CoAtNet input is resized from the same 336-pixel cache. The specialist replaces the generalist on its four columns. After rank normalization:

```text
Four specialist-owned columns: (specialist + CoAtNet + second DINO) / 3
Other eight columns:            (generalist + CoAtNet + second DINO) / 3
```

## Diagnostics on the expert-labeled development panel

These are OOF predictions on the 58 expert-labeled studies: each study uses its held-out checkpoint from each recipe before composition. They are not predictions from all five checkpoints on every gold study. There are only 9–35 positives per finding, so the intervals are wide.

“Report target AUC” means the report-derived target scored against the expert labels on this panel. The difference from image-model AUC is descriptive; I do not think its sign alone identifies whether supervision or representation is the bottleneck.

| Finding | Positives | Image-model AUC (95% CI) | Report target AUC |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| MCL | 9 | 0.980 [0.932, 1.000] | 0.921 |
| Baker's | 12 | 0.958 [0.892, 1.000] | 0.902 |
| ACL | 24 | 0.958 [0.893, 1.000] | 0.944 |
| Medial OA | 15 | 0.950 [0.889, 0.992] | 0.891 |
| Medial Meniscus | 26 | 0.947 [0.888, 0.990] | 0.927 |
| Contusion | 19 | 0.915 [0.826, 0.981] | 0.821 |
| Effusion | 35 | 0.901 [0.804, 0.971] | 0.696 |
| Fracture | 18 | 0.875 [0.756, 0.969] | 0.814 |
| Lateral Meniscus | 23 | 0.858 [0.746, 0.949] | 0.894 |
| PF OA | 21 | 0.824 [0.696, 0.924] | 0.819 |
| Lateral OA | 11 | 0.782 [0.575, 0.954] | 0.829 |
| Synovitis | 27 | 0.693 [0.544, 0.824] | 0.676 |

Two observations are motivating my next experiments:

- **Synovitis supervision is sparse.** My extractor classifies 3,610 of 4,407 reports (about 82%) as `not_mentioned`. Overall, 3,745 Synovitis targets (about 85%) are masked, including uncertain cases. Separately, my report audit found that 12 of 27 expert-positive studies had no explicit Synovitis statement. This limits what direct extraction can recover from those reports; it does not establish the image model's ceiling.
- **Lateral findings remain difficult.** The image-model AUC is below the report-target AUC for Lateral OA and Lateral Meniscus. For Lateral OA, 10 of 11 expert-positive studies mention the finding in their reports. This motivates looking at image construction and training, but does not rule out problems with target quality or disease definitions.

## Experiments that did not provide a useful further gain

Longer schedules and the specialist update have helped; by increasing the training epochs from 25 to 50, the AUC score raised from 0.899 to 0.903 on the public LB. The experiments below did not provide a convincing further gain in the recipes I tested.

- **Alternative public labels:** I tried [Steven's public LLM labels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stevenleehans/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels). Better target AUC on gold58 did not translate into a convincing image-model improvement in my tested recipe. I do not regard target-quality differences as predicted model gains.
- **Explicit 2×2 spatial region tokens:** I appended pooled regional features to the label-query attention. At 50 epochs, the paired composition gain over two folds was **+0.000003**, with 95% CI **[−0.00086,+0.00084]**. This recipe did not help; I have not tested anatomical segmentation supervision.
- **Earlier DINOv3-B trials:** These were unsuccessful under an older pipeline. However, the configurations differed in preprocessing, supervision and training settings, so I do not regard them as a controlled conclusion about DINOv3 or about freezing versus fine-tuning.

## Questions I would appreciate help with

1. **Study construction:** For strong single-model results, what mattered most: series selection, physical crop, slice coverage or sampling? What would you check first in the images actually reaching the model? In 2.5D inputs, have you compared consecutive source slices with neighbors in a sparsely sampled stack?

2. **Weak supervision:** How do you handle report-silent and uncertain findings? Have masking, weighting or objective changes helped more than further extraction work?

3. **Compact CNNs:** For competitors doing well with ResNet, EfficientNet or ConvNeXt, which broad training choices mattered most? I am running a matched ConvNeXt-Tiny experiment before spending compute on larger inputs.

4. **Validation:** How do you decide whether a small gain against noisy report-derived labels is worth pursuing while limiting dependence on the public leaderboard?

Thanks to everyone sharing experiments. The recent threads on [fold count](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/740375) and compact models prompted this post. Even high-level observations about what to audit or test next would be helpful.

If any of this is useful to you, I'd genuinely enjoy comparing notes — especially with anyone working on MRI preprocessing, weak supervision, or a modelling approach different from mine. 

**I'm also looking for teammates!** If anyone would like to join my team — or would have me join yours — please let me know. I'd bring this pipeline and the full ablation history behind it, including the experiments that didn't work. Everything here was trained on my own GPU.

Some thoughts: take the best scoring single model public notebook (ignore the blends) and reproduce it locally. Use public LLM labels if you don't have your own, especially those that have documented extraction processes. Ideally you use your own so you know exactly where they succeed and where they fail. 

Start with 224px / 288px and a simple CNN encoder, like a ResNet34 or EffNetB0. No attention mechanisms, just use simple pooling operations. You can score in the 0.94+ range with this alone and it allows for efficient experiments at the lower resolutions.

Validate against the report extracted labels, not the provided 58 labels and not against the LB - neither are large enough sample sizes to resolve 0.002-0.003 differences. You want to stack these small improvements. Set a CV threshold for what is a genuine improvement and what is noise. Mine is around 0.003. You can get this tighter running multiple seeds if you need. When you get a real improvement, submit to LB to establish a CV - LB correlation.

This is your baseline. Then ablate through the standard image augmentation stacks. Many of these are generic and many are MRI specific, which you can get from previous competitions. Change one thing at a time so you can isolate what helped and what did not.

Then, you can try different backbones and resolutions, to see if the additional training time is really worth it.

After all of that, you can start trying more "experimental" mechanisms like attention and/or newer image encoders. I have yet to try any DINO inits and based on some preliminary experiments, I have a low prior for it matching standard ImageNet init backbones, but I could be wrong.

Kaggle public code section has been sullied with AI slop as people medal farm. Be cautious of this. There are only a few useful notebooks out there ([like this one](https://www.kaggle.com/code/dreaddevelopment/knee-mri-training-the-twelve-finding-model)). I generally assume a contrarian position about public notebooks - they are likely overly complex and not properly "built up" from simple baselines, using a clean CV protocol. Use them as their own baselines, and prune them to see what is actually useful and what is uneeded. "Prime" your own LLM saying something like "this code is probably over engineered, how can I simplify it?"

Last point - spend a lot of time just thinking about the problem. Have brainstorm sessions with your LLM of choice, without building anything. Stream of conciousness type chats. These "vibe chatting" sessions are where I get most of my ideas - LLMs may not be particularly creative in the context of Kaggle competitions, but they are great for organizing thoughts and finding ideas in that structure, that you might have otherwise not noticed yourself.

Excellent advice thank you for taking the time to share. I can also second that a simple baseline will take you far if done carefully OP (also have 0.94+ at 224px with small simple model). Follow this post and you'll get there!

Now it's just overflowing with AI slop and needlessly complex brute forcing lb attempts. So much compute and so much noise. It's such a shame.

DINO is not a model, it's a way of pretraining that basically teaches a model to match crops of itself. It works on any architecture. DINO v1 even released a ResNet50. I am guessing you are using DINOv2 which is ViT-only. So comparing DINOv2 to a ResNet changes the backbone, the objective, and the pretraining data all at once.

Seems like you also compared a LB result with a CV result. 0.86 CV could score 0.95 on the public leaderboard - everyone has different labels so I can't tell you what a CV of 0.86 means. Use the same fold split and find the CV between your models to compare them.

"DINO crop matching pretraining objective creates a useful prior for MRI classication" is a very different claim from "ViTs are better at MRI classifciation than standard CNNs" and using DINOv2 mixes both at the same time.

Hi Tucker, thanks for the detailed reply — this is exactly the kind of clarification I needed.

    You're right on all three points:

        DINO ≠ DINOv2: I was sloppy. I meant DINOv2 (ViT-S/14) specifically, and I now see the comparison against ResNet changes three things at once: backbone (ViT vs CNN), pretraining objective (DINOv2 self-supervised vs ImageNet supervised), and pretraining data (LVD-142M vs ImageNet-1k). Any of those alone could explain the gap.

        LB vs CV: You're completely right, and this is the more embarrassing mistake. The 0.932 is my public LB score, while the 0.86 is a local CV on my own fold — I shouldn't have compared them at all. 0.86 CV could easily correspond to a very different LB number, exactly as you said. I'll only compare models on the same fold split from now on.

        "DINO prior for MRI" vs "ViT > CNN": Yeah, I was conflating them. Since I've only tried DINOv2-ViT against supervised-ResNet, I can't attribute the gap to either factor.

    My plan to disentangle this:

        Run ResNet50 with DINOv1 self-supervised pretraining (Meta released that checkpoint) on the same fold split, same preprocessing, same labels, evaluated purely on CV.

        Also run a supervised ViT (e.g. vit_small_patch16_224.augreg_in1k from timm) under the identical setup.

I'm wondering whether the older DINOv1 objective is strong enough to matter here, or whether it's really the DINOv2 improvements (larger curated data, better augmentation recipe) that make the difference.

If you say "well maybe DINOv1 isn't good here but DINOv2 and DINOv3 are", which is a valid question as they are all different pretraining protocols, look for sets of models that have both ImageNet and the newer DINOs. title: Synovitis and Effusion Help

messages.text: My worst labelling issues have been with synovitis and effusion. I tested few pipelines against the expert labels and have been getting around 0.7 AUC/75% accuracy no matter how hard I try. Could anyone spare some advice on how to increase AUC and accuracy?

I joined this competition about a week ago and I'm still struggling with the same two labels. Here are my results on the 58 expert-labelled studies (accuracy uses a 50% confidence threshold):

| | Effusion AUC / Acc | Synovitis AUC / Acc |
|---|---|---|
| LLM, reports only | 0.835 / 0.707 | 0.799 / 0.741 |
| LLM, reports + MRI | ~0.91-0.92 / 0.845 | ~0.84-0.86 / 0.69-0.72 |
| Image model trained on my pseudo-labels | 0.986 / 0.931 | 0.859 / 0.776 |

An AUC of around 0.7 with ~75% accuracy makes me wonder whether your pipeline outputs hard 0/1 labels. Since AUC measures ranking, asking for probabilities might help, e.g. ranking roughly "explicitly present" > "equivocal" > "not mentioned" > "explicitly absent". This could improve AUC without necessarily changing accuracy.

In my extraction, ~73% of the training reports say nothing about synovitis. My prompt treats silence as weak evidence of absence, while using effusion, trauma, degeneration, and age as context rather than simply defaulting to a negative label.

The report negatives also don't always agree with the expert labels. Among the 58 studies:

- Synovitis not mentioned: 11/36 (31%) were positive according to the experts.
- Effusion reported as absent/normal: 10/26 (38%) were positive.
- Effusion reported as equivocal/small: 14/18 (78%) were positive.

The expert panel calls fluid positive more often than the reports do. Adding images helped substantially with effusion: 0.835 -> ~0.92 for the LLM, and 0.986 for the image model trained on the pseudo-labels. Synovitis improved much less. My guess is that synovium and fluid are difficult to distinguish on non-contrast MRI, so the image input may have led the LLM to predict synovitis more often than the experts did.

Thank you so much, also, im assuming that you are using pseudolabelling to train a better model. How would you trust the synovitis labels when most models usually get around 70-80% accuracy on the synovitis labels?

Yes, it's pseudo-labelling. To be honest, I don't fully trust the synovitis labels either, and it's my weakest label as well.

I train on soft probabilities rather than 0/1, so uncertain cases stay around 0.3-0.6 instead of being forced to one side. Since the metric is AUC, ranking matters more than accuracy at 0.5, and labels with ~75% accuracy can still rank reasonably well.

For effusion, the noise largely averages out and the image model ends up better than its labels. Synovitis doesn't benefit as much, so I'm still looking for ways to reduce the noise in the synovitis labels and make them more accurate.
Also, How did you get effusion accuracy so high?
