title: "Not addressed" is a label too — what we learned reading 4,407 knee reports with an LLM

messages.text:
**TL;DR** — Only 58 of 4,407 training studies have real labels, so everyone manufactures
targets from the radiology report. An LLM does this measurably better than a regex
(**0.8780 vs 0.8136** against the 58 gold studies). But the more useful finding is about
the *gaps*: **25.4% of all label cells are "the report does not address this"**, and what
that silence *means* is different for every finding. Getting that wrong costs more than the
labeller's accuracy does.

---

## Credit

**LLM-read report labels are not our idea, and we were not first.** Several people
published them before us, and anyone arriving at this post should have their work too:

- **Pilkwang Kim** — [rsna-knee-llm-labels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels)
  (2026-08-06, the first of these) and
  [rsna-knee-baseline-v1](https://www.kaggle.com/code/pilkwang/rsna-knee-baseline-v1)
- **barun2104** — [Stratified Folds & LLM Soft Labels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/barun2104/rsna-knee-stratified-folds-and-llm-soft-labels) (2026-08-07)
- **lixin73** — [LLM Report Labels (GPT-5.6-Sol)](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/lixin73/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels-sol56) (2026-08-08)

And the pipelines this work was measured against:

- **Karnakbayev Artur** — [rsna-knee-eda-to-2-5d](https://www.kaggle.com/code/karnakbaevarthur/rsna-knee-eda-to-2-5d)
- **Will / wguesdon** — [rsna-knee-dinov2-at-meniscus-resolution](https://www.kaggle.com/code/wguesdon/rsna-knee-dinov2-at-meniscus-resolution)
- **Alexandre Moritz**, **Roman Rozen** — public EDA and baselines

The observation that *labels*, not the encoder, are the binding constraint came from
measuring their pipelines — not from improving on them.

**So what is this post for?** Not the labelling. It is about what the labeller does when it
*refuses* to answer, which is a quarter of the time, and which we have not seen discussed.
If you already use one of the label sets above, section 4 is the part that may change what
you do with it.

---

## 1. The setup, for anyone arriving late

`train.csv` has a `Report` column. `test.csv` does not. So text can only ever produce
**targets**, never a model input. And only **58 of 4,407** studies carry real annotator
labels for the twelve findings — 1.3%.

That means almost everyone in this competition is training against labels they invented,
and the quality of that invention is a ceiling nothing downstream can pass.

Measured against those 58 gold studies:

| label source | macro AUC vs gold |
|---|---|
| regex / lexicon extraction | 0.8136 |
| LLM reading the same reports | **0.8780** |

We published the labels: **[RSNA Knee LLM Report Labels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/stevenleehans/rsna-knee-llm-report-labels)**.

---

## 2. The part we did not expect

We asked the labeller for a probability per finding, **with an explicit "the report does
not address this" option** that maps to 0.5. That turned out to be the most informative
design decision we made, because it makes the *gaps* visible instead of silently coercing
them to negative.

**25.4% of all cells came back at exactly 0.5.** And they are wildly uneven:

| finding | gold AUC | "not addressed" |
|---|---|---|
| **Synovitis** | **0.678** | **83.7%** |
| Baker's | 0.946 | 48.2% |
| Fracture | 0.793 | 42.9% |
| ACL | 0.993 | 8.3% |
| Medial Meniscus | 0.954 | 5.5% |

**Synovitis is the worst column by a distance — and 84% of it is missing.** Yet 27 of the
58 gold studies *have* synovitis. It is common in the joint and seldom written down.
The labeller is being honest, and the honesty destroys the column.

---

## 3. One thing we tested, and it worked

Radiologists report **effusion** readily and **synovitis** rarely, and the two co-occur.
So we asked a single pre-registered question: does the *Effusion* field predict *gold
Synovitis* better than the *Synovitis* field does?

```
LLM Synovitis field  vs gold Synovitis : 0.6780
LLM Effusion  field  vs gold Synovitis : 0.7115   <-- yes
gold co-occurrence: P(syn | eff) = 0.63  vs  P(syn | no eff) = 0.22
```

**A field that is not about synovitis predicts synovitis better than the synovitis field
does.** Filling only the *undecided* synovitis cells from effusion — never overriding an
explicit statement — moves that column **0.678 → 0.790** and the whole key
**0.8780 → 0.8873**.

---

## 4. The part worth your attention: generalising it made things worse

The obvious next move is to do that for all twelve findings. So we did, properly: for each
finding, learn a ridge model predicting it from the other eleven, **fit on the 4,407-study
corpus** (never on the 58 gold — those were used only to score, once), and use it to fill
that finding's undecided cells.

| key | macro vs gold |
|---|---|
| v1 baseline | 0.8780 |
| **v2 — synovitis only** | **0.8873** |
| v3 — learned imputation, all twelve | 0.8805 |

**The blanket version is worse than the targeted one.** Per label it splits cleanly:

```
Synovitis  +0.056     Baker's   -0.029
PF OA      +0.023     Contusion -0.031
Fracture   +0.015     Lateral OA -0.019
```

Here is why, and it is the actual lesson:

| finding | gold+ when report is SILENT | when it SPEAKS |
|---|---|---|
| Synovitis | **0.34** | 0.76 |
| PF OA | 0.21 | 0.41 |
| Baker's | **0.03** | 0.44 |
| Medial OA | **0.00** | 0.36 |

**When a radiologist does not mention a Baker's cyst, there almost certainly is not one —
3% versus 44%. The silence *is* the label.** Overwriting it with a correlation-based guess
throws away real information. But silence about synovitis still leaves a 34% chance it is
present, so there the silence is genuinely uninformative and imputing helps.

Across the nine readable findings, that "silence ratio" correlates **+0.59** with how much
imputation helped. (Nine points — suggestive, not proven.)

> **"Not addressed" is not one thing. For some findings it means *absent*; for others it
> means *nobody looked*. Treating them alike is worse than leaving the gaps in.**

---

## 5. Honest limits

- **58 studies is a small ruler.** On it, differences below roughly 0.02 macro are not
  measurable. We have had three separate readings from this ruler overturned by the
  leaderboard — treat small gaps as *unknown*, not as zero.
- **A better key is not automatically a better model.** We swapped these labels in and got
  no gain on the first attempt; it only paid off after unrelated pipeline bugs were fixed.
- **We also tried the version that cheats** — selecting *which* findings to impute using the
  gold labels. It scored 0.8845, still below the disciplined 0.8873. Nothing was left on the
  table by not cheating, which is not always how that goes.
- **Gold prevalence is the annotator's sampling, not disease prevalence.** Every gold study
  has at least one positive finding; mean 4.14 per study.
- These are **model-generated labels, not ground truth** — a better approximation of what
  the report says, nothing more.

---

## 6. If you take one thing

Ask your labeller for **"I don't know"** as a first-class answer, then look at where it
says so. The distribution of its refusals told us more about this dataset than its accuracy
did — and one column, repaired on that basis, was worth more than any change we made to the

title: Slice order in the public baseline is basically random (worth +0.028 AUC)

messages.text:
I was working from one of the shared baselines and ran into something that I think affects most of the forks.

read_slot() builds the slice stack with sorted(filename). The filenames are SOP Instance UIDs, so that order has nothing to do with anatomy.

I checked it on 60 random series, comparing filename order against ImagePositionPatient projected on the axis with most variation:

median |Spearman rho| 0.164, 0.0% of series above 0.9, 98.3% below 0.5. Nothing reversed either, so it is not a flipped-stack problem, it is just shuffled.

Two things follow from that. The "central 60% of the stack" that read_slot samples is not the middle of the knee, it is 9 arbitrary positions. And the 3 slices stacked as channels are not neighbours. Also normalise_laterality() flips sagittal stacks for right knees, and that flip only means something if the order was right to begin with.

What I measured, one fold, same seed, same folds, 12 epochs, nothing else changed: filename order 0.7695, IPP order 0.7971, so +0.0276.

I also ran the patched version again with a different seed, just to see how much of that is noise: 0.7960. So seed noise is around 0.001 and the effect is about 25x that.

The fix is just sorting by ImagePositionPatient along the through-plane axis, with InstanceNumber as a fallback. One warning if you try it: do it inside read_slot and cache it per series. I first put it in probe() and it ended up reading headers for all ~820k files, which added about 7 minutes to every run before I noticed.

Happy to share the cell if anyone wants it.

title: Rules clarification: external knee-MRI datasets, and using an LLM API to derive labels from the reports

messages.text:
1. Do external knee-MRI datasets with free research-use agreements count as "publicly available and equally accessible at no cost"?

The rules permit external data that is freely and publicly available to all participants. The main public knee-MRI resources — MRNet (Stanford), fastMRI+ (NYU), the Osteoarthritis Initiative, and SKM-TEA — are all free of charge, but each requires registering and accepting a research-use agreement before download. None of them charge, and none restrict access to a particular institution, but the click-through step means they aren't anonymously downloadable.

Does that satisfy the "equally accessible at no cost" condition? A yes/no on the category would be more useful than a ruling on any single dataset, since the same access pattern covers essentially every public MSK-MRI resource.

Related: does the answer change for pretrained weights released under a research-use agreement rather than a permissive licence, given the winners' obligation to open-source code and weights under CC-BY-NC 4.0?

2. Is it permitted to send the training reports to a commercial LLM API in order to derive labels from them?

The competition explicitly suggests deriving labels for the unlabeled studies from the report text, and the reports are in nine languages, so a multilingual LLM is the natural tool. But the data-security rule says competition data must not be provided to anyone who has not accepted the rules, and it isn't obvious to me whether sending report text to a third-party API for inference counts as "providing data" or simply as using a tool.

Concretely, is either of these permitted?

(a) Sending report text to a hosted LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, etc.) during development, with the derived labels used purely as a training artifact — no report text and no API access at submission time.
(b) Same, but with an open-weights model run locally or in a Kaggle notebook, so the text never leaves the participant's own environment.
I assume (b) is fine and am mainly asking about (a). If (a) is not permitted, that's very much worth everyone knowing before they build on it — and if it is, saying so publicly puts teams without local GPU capacity on the same footing as those with it.

However, there is already a problem: label datasets derived using GPT have been publicly shared on the platform. Other public datasets may likewise have been labeled with commercial LLMs. If using such datasets is to be considered a rule violation, I don't see how the competition hosts or Kaggle staff could realistically make that determination for any given dataset. 2.6(a) is a disjunction: External Data must be "either publicly available and equally accessible ... at no cost to the other Participants, **or** satisfies the Reasonableness criteria as outlined in Section 2.6.b."

And 2.6.b states that "the use of external data and models is acceptable **unless specifically prohibited by the Host**," with the Reasonableness Standard aimed at excessive cost and geo restrictions.

**2. title: PSA: bf16 on Kaggle's T4/P100 silently cost me 0.14 AUC (0.851 → 0.710). How to spot it.

messages.text:
My own model scored **0.710** public, while held-out evaluation on the 58 annotated studies said ~0.86. It wasn't the model. Here's what happened, in case it saves someone a week.

**What went wrong**
- My inference kernel used `torch.autocast(dtype=torch.bfloat16)`, copied from training on an A100.
- T4 and P100 have no bf16 units. PyTorch doesn't error: it **emulates**, and each forward pass got ~50x slower (~0.9 s per model pass per study for a ViT-S with 24 images).
- 10 checkpoints x 5 TTA views = 50 passes per study, x 1,322 hidden studies = ~17 hours.
- My kernel has a time guard (stop at 8 h and write a prior of 0.5 for whatever isn't done). It hit the guard after ~620 studies, so **more than half the test got a constant 0.5**. That scores ~0.71 for a model that's really ~0.86.
- On the 3 visible test studies, everything looked fine. The failure only exists at hidden-test scale.

**The fix:** `dtype=torch.float16` (T4 has fp16 tensor cores). Same model, resubmitted: **0.851**.

**Checklist for your own kernel**
1. `torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()` on the scoring GPU. If it's False, don't autocast to bf16.
2. Log seconds per study, and extrapolate to ~1,300 hidden studies *plus* headroom, before trusting a public score.
3. If you have a time guard with a fallback, log how many studies hit the fallback. A silent partial fallback looks exactly like a bad model.
4. To tell "bad model" from "bad pipeline", run your exact inference path on held-out *train* studies (DICOM -> decode -> TTA -> rank) and score it against the annotated ones. Mine gave 0.858 there, which is how I knew the leaderboard number was wrong.

---

Separately: I have an **independent arm** (DINOv2 ViT-S, 6 series x 16 slices over 140 mm at 336 px, fully fine-tuned, 5 folds) that shares no weights with the public ensemble. If you're at **0.945+** and want an uncorrelated component before the 15 Oct merge deadline, happy to talk.
As far as I understand, the P100 and T4 GPUs do not support bfloat16.
Good catch! You need to use `torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported(including_emulation=False)` though as the default may still output `true` depending on torch version.

title: What is difference between study and series?

messages.text:
I will offer my layman understanding of this. All the series within a study represents a single person. So why multiple series? Well, each series tries to provide different evidence, or makes it easier to identify different abnormalities.

Within a study, three different views of the knee are taken: side view (sagittal), front view (coronal) and bottom view (axial). Each of these planes provides the reviewer a different angle to look for an abnormality. This is because an abnormality may only be visible when looking at it from one particular view (which you can't tell beforehand when performing the MRI scan). 

Each of these three planes may also have different properties such as fat suppression and fluid sensitivity. A normal MRI will make fat appear bright, which can make it sometimes difficult to differentiate fat from fluids. A fat suppressed series only allows fluids to look bright while suppressing fats from appearing bright. This makes it easier to identify abnormalities related to fluids such as effusion and synovitis. See the hosts's post [here](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/rsna-knee-abnormality-detection/discussion/733343) for more on this.

The slices in a series may also vary by thickness. Series with many slices will typically have thinner slices. If you consider all these variations (view, fat suppression, fluid sensitivity, and thickness), it's not difficult to see why a study can have up to 14 series. A sagittal series may have fat suppression or not. The same sagittal series may have different slice thickness as well.

In order to make a judgment about a knee abnormality, the reviewer will need to see all these series (different angles, different fat and fluid configurations) in order to have a holistic understanding of the knee's condition.

Thanks, Chris. I tested the report/E11 signals as a small, controlled first step. Only 57 matched gold-labeled studies were available per finding across the 12 targets, so these local results are noisy and are not leaderboard scores. They also do not measure my complete ensemble, whose current public score is 0.940.

Validation results (mean macro AUC):
• Report-only: 0.8692
• E11 OOF-only: 0.8582
• Fixed 50/50 percentile-rank blend: 0.9077
• Nested-CV-tuned rank weights: 0.9026
• Raw 50/50 probability mean: 0.9105
• Train-standardized mean: 0.9086

The weight-tuned rank blend was worse than the fixed blend. Raw averaging was only +0.0028 over percentile ranking on this small sample, so I did not change the 0.940 submission. The rank-weight experiment used nested CV (outer 3-fold × 10 repeats; inner 3-fold × 3 repeats for weight selection); the signal-transform comparison used repeated 3-fold validation × 10. These tests cover only the report/E11 branch; I still need OOF predictions from the full ensemble to evaluate a real addition.

Next I plan to audit report labels, then test one MRI preprocessing or input-representation change at a time, followed by a different backbone or augmentation/schedule if validation supports it. Practical tips: keep all slices/series from each study in one fold; inspect per-target AUC as well as macro AUC; generate full-ensemble OOF predictions before blending; tune weights only inside training folds; and repeat apparent gains across folds/seeds before trusting them. I’ll avoid choosing changes based only on public leaderboard movement.

Which preprocessing or representation change would you try first for this dataset?

My notebook is an attributed reproduction of Mattia Angeli’s public version 27, ‘Bend the Knee to the DINOv3.’ It includes 20 DINO MRI members, five DINOv3/A5 folds, RadImageNet heads, and probability-based TTA pooling with target-specific overrides. For those who improved beyond 0.94, what helped most: better report-derived labels, a genuinely different encoder, or OOF-based ensemble blending? How did you validate changes without overfitting to the public leaderboard? I’ll retain attribution for any code or ideas I use.
Try blending some other model with this to increase the score

Thanks, Lavin! I already have a blended ensemble with DINO-family MRI models and RadImageNet heads, so I’ll focus on adding a genuinely complementary model and validate the blend with OOF predictions rather than tuning to the public leaderboard. Did you have a particular backbone or checkpoint that worked well for this dataset?

Relying on OOF predictions rather than chasing the public leaderboard is absolutely the right move, especially for preventing overfitting on medical datasets.
Since the current ensemble relies heavily on self-supervised, vision-transformer-based representations via DINO and RadImageNet, the most effective way to gain a genuine performance boost is by introducing a backbone with a completely different structural bias.
A ConvNeXt-V2 (specifically convnextv2_huge or large) or a Swin Transformer V2 initialized with masked autoencoder (MAE) weights would be excellent complementary choices.

The short answer: the text round-trip can't add information, only lose it. At inference you have pixels and nothing else. Image -> generated report -> extracted labels is image -> labels with a lossy text bottleneck inserted in the middle. Whatever the VLM can see, a classifier trained directly on the same pixels can also see, without the generation and re-extraction steps each contributing their own errors.

The one version that isn't circular is using image -> text as pretraining - train the encoder to match report embeddings, then fine-tune a label head on top. I tested the premise of that and it failed: a linear probe on BGE-M3 embeddings of the reports (PCA to 128 dims) scored 0.8423 on 58 gold, against 0.8843 for LLM+regex extraction on the same studies. The embedding carried less retrievable label signal than twelve extracted numbers - much worse on MCL (0.78 vs 0.95) and lateral meniscus (0.78 vs 0.89), marginally better on contusion and fracture, all within the ±0.02 that 58 studies carry. I dropped the idea on that result.

Two things I measured that might be more useful to you:

Swapping the LLM is worth nothing. On all 58 gold: qwen2.5:14b rev4 0.8619, qwen3:14b 0.8572, qwen3:30b-a3b 0.8677. A 0.010 spread on 58 studies is noise. Watch out for reasoning models - qwen3's <think> block collides with JSON-constrained decoding and silently eats answers (12/58 and 52/58 unparsed until we turned thinking off).

Extraction is closer to its ceiling than it looks. I audited every gold positive, report score missed and asked whether the report contains any term for that finding, negation ignored. Extraction caught 207 of 240 positives, and 22 of the 33 misses were reports that never name the finding at all - synovitis, fracture and effusion miss only on silent reports. No reader recovers text that was never written, and neither will a VLM.

Given your labels already read 0.9083 on gold, I'd guess extraction isn't where your remaining headroom is either.

Reciprocating with a question, since your 0.935 on a single fold is well ahead of where I am: how many slices per series are you caching, and how many 2.5D windows do you feed per series? I measured mine corpus at median 30 slices per series (p90 39, p99 160), and going from 24 to 32 cached slices - 69% to 84% of all slices retained - was worth more to me than anything I did to the labels.

If that extraction score comes from single shot and not a weighted blend then I think thats the highest match with the data that I have heard on gold. Labels shouldnt be your setback. There are a number of teams who have reported taking effnet b0 to 0.94+ on LB with 5 fold ensemble + TTA with 0.88 AUC on extraction labels. I obviously dont know anything about your pipeline but I would say your inference may give you more in TTA + 5 fold. And there is probably a bit of headroom in modeling or unique tricks from that point that I dont think have gone public in detail like pseudo labels? But it sounds like you are at the edge of top public knowledge. I can save you the GPU hours and say confidently that it shouldnt be your labels.

title: From AlexNet to DINOv3: A Practical Backbone History for the RSNA Knee MRI 2026 Challenge

messages.text: Nice history. The current SOTA are working best for this competition.
They are only working well if you have strong labels. The public `GPT 5.6` labelled data got me to .910 with a simple Resnet34 using a mundane linear head with no augmentations.

- When you open the attached PDF, you can access the embedded links. -

Author: Sean Lee, Graph‑Axis‑AI Grounded.
Prepared: 2026‑09‑08

Introduction

I have been reviewing the model families that are currently relevant to the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection
2026 competition, not only as a list of backbones, but as an architectural history: who developed each family,
what problem it was designed to solve, what changed from the previous generation, and whether that
change is actually useful for knee MRI.
The competition is a particularly interesting test bed for this question. The official task is to predict 12 knee
abnormalities at the study level from MRI studies consisting of multiple DICOM series. The dataset is interna‑
tional, multi‑site, multi‑scanner and multi‑protocol, and the training data also includes multilingual radiology
reports. RSNA describes the challenge as its first knee MRI AI challenge and its first challenge to combine medical
images with multilingual report text.
• Kaggle competition: Source
• Kaggle dataset description: Source
• RSNA challenge page: Source
• RSNA 2026 announcement: Source
My current conclusion is that the question “Which backbone is best?” is too narrow.
For this competition, the final performance is more likely to come from the interaction of:
DICOM physical normalization
+ series/plane selection
+ slice sampling
+ study‑level aggregation
+ report‑derived supervision
+ target‑specific pooling/heads
+ an efficient backbone
rather than from simply replacing one backbone with a larger one.
My current primary candidate remains DINOv2‑Small, with ResNet34 as a control model, while newer or
alternative families such as DINOv3, ConvNeXt, EfficientNetV2, ResNeXt, Swin Transformer, MAE and
RadImageNet‑pretrained CNNs are worth controlled ablation rather than automatic promotion to the main
model.

2. CNN Lineage: From AlexNet to ConvNeXt
The modern CNN era was accelerated by AlexNet, which demonstrated that a deep convolutional network
trained with GPUs could dramatically improve large‑scale image recognition.
VGG then showed that a very regular architecture built from repeated 3×3 convolutions could scale effectively
with depth.
• VGG: Source
Google’s Inception / GoogLeNet took another direction: instead of using a single filter scale, it processed fea‑
tures through multiple branches and scales in parallel.
• GoogLeNet / Inception: Source
The major next step was ResNet. Its residual formulation,
2
y = F(x) + x
made much deeper networks substantially easier to optimize.
• ResNet: Source
For the current competition, ResNet34 is especially useful as a control model. It is simple, stable, memory‑
efficient and easy to adapt to 2.5D slice stacks. It also gives us a clean way to determine whether an improvement
came from the backbone itself or from preprocessing, labels, sampling or aggregation.
DenseNet introduced dense connectivity, where each layer receives features from all preceding layers. This
improves feature reuse and gradient flow, but the concatenation pattern can increase activation‑memory traffic.
• DenseNet: Source
ResNeXt extended the residual idea by introducing cardinality: multiple parallel transformations with the same
topology, efficiently implemented with grouped convolutions.
• ResNeXt: Source
EfficientNet then focused on coordinated scaling of network depth, width and input resolution instead of scal‑
ing them independently.
• EfficientNet: Source
The later EfficientNetV2 incorporated training speed directly into the design objective and introduced Fused‑
MBConv blocks.
• EfficientNetV2: Source
RegNet is also interesting for Kaggle because it came from studying the design space of networks rather than
searching for one isolated architecture. FAIR reported that some RegNet variants could outperform EfficientNet
under comparable FLOPs while running substantially faster on GPUs.
• RegNet: Source
Finally, ConvNeXt asked a very useful question: if we modernize ResNet using lessons learned during the Trans‑
former era, how far can a pure CNN still go?
• ConvNeXt: Source
For this challenge, I consider ConvNeXt‑Tiny one of the most useful additional CNN controls because it helps
separate the question of Transformer superiority from the effect of modern training and architectural design.
3. Transformer and Self‑Supervised Lineage: ViT ‑> MAE / DINO ‑> DINOv2
‑> DINOv3
The Vision Transformer (ViT) replaced convolutional feature extraction with a sequence of image patches pro‑
cessed by a Transformer.
• ViT: Source
DeiT then showed that ViTs could be trained much more data‑efficiently than the original large‑scale ViT recipe
suggested.
• DeiT: Source
BEiT adapted BERT‑style masked modeling to images.
• BEiT: Source
MAE simplified this idea further: mask a very large fraction of image patches, encode only the visible subset and
reconstruct the missing content.
• MAE: Source
3
This is particularly relevant to medical imaging because unlabeled DICOM data is far easier to obtain than expert
labels. A future medical pipeline could therefore use large‑scale self‑supervised MRI pretraining before task‑
specific fine‑tuning.
DINOv2, introduced by Meta AI, is a self‑supervised visual foundation model trained to produce broadly trans‑
ferable visual representations.
• DINOv2 paper: Source
For the current RSNA Knee competition, DINOv2‑Small remains attractive because it offers strong representa‑
tion quality without the computational cost of much larger variants.
The direct successor, DINOv3, was released by Meta in 2025. Meta scaled self‑supervised learning much further
and introduced changes intended to preserve strong dense visual features during large‑scale training.
• DINOv3 overview: Source
• DINOv3 research page: Source
However, newer does not automatically mean better for this competition.
A fair DINOv2‑S vs DINOv3‑S comparison should keep everything else fixed:
• identical DICOM preprocessing,
• identical physical crop,
• identical slice sampling,
• identical resolution,
• identical cross‑series aggregator,
• identical target heads,
• identical folds and training budget.
Only then can we tell whether the representation itself is better for this task.
4. Swin Transformer and the Medical 3D Branch
Swin Transformer, developed by Microsoft Research, introduced hierarchical representations and shifted‑
window attention.
• Swin Transformer: Source
This matters because medical imaging is not naturally a collection of unrelated 2D photographs. MRI contains
local structure, global anatomical context, multiple planes and ordered slices.
The medical‑imaging community extended Transformer ideas into 3D architectures such as UNETR and Swin
UNETR.
• UNETR: Source
• Swin UNETR: Source
These models are mainly segmentation architectures rather than direct replacements for a study‑level 12‑label
classifier. Still, their history is relevant because they demonstrate how hierarchical Transformer representations
can be adapted to volumetric medical data.
5. U‑Net and nnU‑Net: Why Medical Imaging Has Its Own Architectural
History
The history of medical imaging cannot be described only through ImageNet backbones.
U‑Net became one of the foundational architectures of biomedical image segmentation because it combined a
contracting encoder with an expanding decoder and skip connections.
4
• U‑Net: Source
nnU‑Net took a different step. Its major contribution was not a new convolution block, but a self‑configuring
pipeline that automatically adapts preprocessing, architecture, training and post‑processing to the dataset.
• nnU‑Net: Source
This is conceptually important for Kaggle as well: sometimes the pipeline and configuration strategy matter
more than inventing a new backbone.
6. RadImageNet: Domain‑Specific Pretraining Deserves a Serious Test
One of themost relevant alternatives for this challenge is not a new architecture at all, but a differentpretraining
domain.
RadImageNet contains about 1.35 million annotated radiologic images across CT, MRI and ultrasound and
provides pretrained versions of ResNet50, DenseNet121, InceptionV3 and InceptionResNetV2.
• RadImageNet paper: Source
• Official repository: Source
The original RadImageNet study reported improvements over ImageNet pretraining on several small medical
datasets, including ACL injury MRI and meniscus tear MRI.
That makes RadImageNet unusually relevant to this particular competition.
A useful experiment would be:
ImageNet‑ResNet50 vs RadImageNet‑ResNet50
under exactly the same knee‑MRI preprocessing, 2.5D input and study‑level aggregation.
This would test pretraining‑domain transfer rather than architecture alone.
7. MONAI: Not My Choice for This Competition, but Potentially a Future
Standard Layer for Medical Imaging AI
I also tested MONAI during my RSNA Knee MRI work.
For this specific competition, my current assessment is that MONAI is not the best fit for the main Kaggle
pipeline. The challenge is dominated by a very specific study‑level classification problem under a strict
notebook runtime budget, with custom DICOM preprocessing, slice selection, multi‑plane aggregation and
lightweight backbone experimentation. In that setting, a more direct PyTorch pipeline has been easier for me
to control, profile and optimize.
This is not a criticism of MONAI itself. MONAI is a PyTorch‑based, open‑source framework designed specifically
for healthcare imaging, with medical‑image transforms, caching, domain‑specific networks and losses, multi‑
GPU support, model bundles, labeling tools and deployment components.
• Project MONAI: Source
• MONAI GitHub: Source
• MONAI Tutorials: Source
• MONAI Documentation: Source
Project MONAI was initiated by NVIDIA and King’s College London and has since grown into a broader medical‑
imaging AI ecosystem. Its architecture is much more relevant to long‑term medical AI development than a sin‑
gle Kaggle competition because it is designed around reusable healthcare‑imaging workflows rather than one
competition‑specific classifier.
My current view is therefore:
5
MONAI is not the framework I would prioritize for maximizing this particular RSNA Knee Kaggle
score today, but I believe MONAI ‑ or a MONAI‑like PyTorch‑native medical‑imaging framework
‑ has a strong chance of becoming an important standard layer for future MRI and DICOM AI
training workflows.
The reasons are structural:
• medical‑image‑aware preprocessing instead of generic computer‑vision transforms,
• native handling of 2D, 2.5D and 3D healthcare‑imaging workflows,
• reusable DICOM/NIfTI‑oriented data pipelines,
• medical‑specific losses, metrics and transforms,
• caching and large‑volume data handling,
• integration with labeling through MONAI Label,
• packaging and reproducibility through MONAI Bundles,
• a path from research code toward deployment.
For future MRI systems, I expect the more important question to become:
DICOM / MRI acquisition
v
medical-image-aware preprocessing
v
MONAI or equivalent medical AI framework
v
PyTorch backbone / foundation model
v
multi-GPU training
v
validation / annotation / deployment
rather than treating every medical imaging project as an isolated collection of custom image‑loading scripts.
So my position is deliberately split:
For this Kaggle competition: custom PyTorch pipeline first.
For future MRI/DICOM training infrastructure: MONAI deserves serious long‑term attention.
This is an empirical opinion from my current testing, not a claim that MONAI is already the universal standard
or that it will necessarily outperform custom pipelines on every task.
8. My Current Practical Model Hierarchy for RSNA Knee 2026
Primary model
DINOv2‑Small
Reason: strong general representation, manageable compute, and a good fit for hierarchical study‑level aggre‑
gation.
Mandatory control
ResNet34
Reason: simple, fast and stable; ideal for determining whether preprocessing or label improvements generalize
independently of backbone choice.
High‑priority additional ablations
• DINOv3‑Small
• ConvNeXt‑Tiny
6
• EfficientNetV2‑S
• ResNeXt50
• RadImageNet‑ResNet50
Secondary research branches
• Swin‑T
• MAE‑pretrained ViT
• CoAtNet
• RadImageNet‑DenseNet121
Medical 3D / localization branch
• U‑Net
• nnU‑Net
• UNETR
• Swin UNETR
These last models should not simply be dropped into the classification pipeline as if they were equivalent back‑
bones. Their more natural role may be ROI localization, segmentation, anatomical supervision or 3D repre‑
sentation learning.
9. The More Important Question: Is the Backbone Really the Bottleneck?
This is where I think the competition becomes more interesting.
A knee MRI study is not a single image. It contains multiple series, different planes, different sequence sensitiv‑
ities and a variable number of slices.
So the full prediction problem is closer to:
DICOM study
v
physical orientation / position ordering
v
scanner- and spacing-aware normalization
v
series / plane selection
v
anatomically meaningful slice sampling
v
shared visual encoder
v
per-series / per-plane pooling
v
cross-series aggregation
v
12 target-specific heads
This means that a better backbone can still lose to a weaker backbone if:
• slices are physically misordered,
• PixelSpacing is ignored,
• the crop represents a different physical field of view across scanners,
• important series are omitted,
• irrelevant end slices dominate sampling,
• all 12 abnormalities are forced to use the same pooling strategy,
7
• or weak labels from reports are poorly calibrated.
That is why I currently view this as a study‑construction and supervision problem first, and a backbone‑
ranking problem second.
10. Debate: Questions I Would Like to Discuss With Other Competitors
Debate 1 ‑ DINOv2 vs DINOv3
Does DINOv3 actually improve knee‑MRI transfer under identical preprocessing and compute, or is the differ‑
ence smaller than the gain from better study construction?
Debate 2 ‑ Generic SSL vs radiology‑domain pretraining
Would a smaller RadImageNet‑pretrained CNN beat a much stronger generic visual foundation model when gold
labels are scarce?
Debate 3 ‑ 2.5D hierarchical models vs full 3D models
Is full 3Dmodeling worth thememory and runtime cost, or does carefully designedmulti‑plane 2.5D aggregation
capture most of the useful anatomical context?
Debate 4 ‑ Backbone scaling vs image resolution
If DINOv2‑Small is already representation‑sufficient, is compute better spent on 336/448 resolution and better
slice coverage than on DINOv2‑Base/Large?
Debate 5 ‑ One pooling rule or target‑specific pooling?
ACL tears, meniscus tears and fractures are focal findings, while osteoarthritis and effusion can be spatially dif‑
fuse. Should all 12 labels really share one aggregation rule?
Debate 6 ‑ Are we optimizing the wrong layer?
If report‑derived supervision and DICOM normalization dominate the error budget, then changing the backbone
may produce much smaller gains than improving labels, physical coordinates and series selection.
Debate 7 ‑ Competition framework vs long‑term medical‑imaging framework
MONAI may add abstraction and workflow overhead that is unnecessary for this particular Kaggle classifier, but
could that same structure become an advantage when moving from competition code to reusable MRI/DICOM
training, annotation and deployment pipelines?
I would be interested in controlled ablations from other competitors, especially experiments that change one
factor at a time while keeping folds, preprocessing and training budget fixed.
11. Suggested Controlled Benchmark
A simple benchmark matrix could look like this:
8
Experiment Backbone / pretraining Purpose
A ResNet34 / ImageNet Stable control
B DINOv2‑S Main SSL baseline
C DINOv3‑S New‑generation SSL test
D ConvNeXt‑T Modern pure‑CNN test
E EfficientNetV2‑S Efficiency test
F ResNet50 / RadImageNet Domain‑pretraining test
G Swin‑T Hierarchical Transformer test
Everything else should remain fixed.
Then separately ablate:
1. physical slice ordering,
2. fixed‑mm crop,
3. 224 ‑> 336/448 resolution,
4. slice coverage,
5. cross‑plane aggregation,
6. target‑specific pooling,
7. report‑label calibration.
This should tell us much more than comparing public leaderboard scores from notebooks with completely dif‑
ferent pipelines.

Closing Thought
My working hypothesis is that the strongest solution will not be defined by a single fashionable backbone.
It will be defined by how well the system preserves the physical and clinical structure of the MRI study, con‑
verts weak multimodal supervision into reliable targets, and then uses a sufficiently strong but computationally
efficient encoder.
For that reason, I would rather compare systems under controlled conditions than rank architectures by gen‑
eration or publication date.
Comments, contradictory ablations and alternative interpretations are welcome.

Thank you. Many other image-processing backbones are also being actively developed. It is important to choose the right backbone for your specific purpose and application. In practice, rather than relying on a single backbone, combining and blending multiple complementary models often delivers better overall performance.

title: [Baseline Notebook] 2.5D ResNet-34 PyTorch Pipeline (Fold 0) | Preprocessed 3D Volumes

messages.text:
Hey Everyone! 👋
To help jumpstart model exploration in the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection Challenge, I've published a complete, end-to-end [PyTorch baseline notebook](https://www.kaggle.com/code/barun2104/baseline-rsna-knee-mri-2-5d-resnet34) using a **2.5D ResNet-34 architecture** trained on Fold 0.

Handling 3D DICOM volumes directly during training can cause severe I/O bottlenecks. To make training fast, clean, and reproducible, this baseline runs off preprocessed, memory-efficient `(24, 160, 160)` volume arrays.

### 💡 Key Notebook Highlights
- **2.5D ResNet-34 Backbone:** Instead of computationally heavy 3D convolutions, we map the 24 depth slices across input channels, adapting ImageNet pre-trained weights to leverage transfer learning.

- **12 Multi-Label Pathology Targets:** Trains directly on all primary targets (`ACL`, `MCL`, `Meniscus tears`, `OA`, `Effusion`, etc.) using `BCEWithLogitsLoss`.

- **Fast Batch Training (AMP FP16):** Uses Automatic Mixed Precision and batch size of 32 for rapid epoch iteration times on Kaggle GPU (T4 / P100).

- **Cross-Validation Metric:** Tracks Mean Macro ROC-AUC across Fold 0.

### 🔗 Related Resources & Datasets
- **📓 Training Notebook:** [[Baseline] RSNA Knee MRI — 2.5D ResNet34](https://www.kaggle.com/code/barun2104/baseline-rsna-knee-mri-2-5d-resnet34)

- **📊 Metadata CSV Dataset:** [RSNA Knee - Stratified Folds & LLM Soft Labels](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/barun2104/rsna-knee-stratified-folds-and-llm-soft-labels)

- **🖼️ Processed 3D Volumes Dataset:** [RSNA Knee MRI - Processed 3D Volumes](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/barun2104/rsna-knee-mri-processed-3d-volumes)

### 🚀 What's Next on the Roadmap?
- **Semi-Supervised Pre-Training:** Leveraging the `pseudo_*` targets in the metadata file to pre-train on unannotated studies before fine-tuning on ground truth folds.

- **Backbone Benchmarking:** Testing EfficientNet and ConvNeXt 2.5D variants.

- **Data Augmentation:** Adding 3D spatial transformations (random flipping, slight rotations, intensity scaling).

Check out the notebook, feel free to fork/copy it for your own experiments, and let me know if you have any feedback or ideas to improve the CV score!

**What model architectures or slice depths are you planning to experiment with first?**
Thanks for sharing!

title: Only 58 Gold Labels.

messages.text: I know maybe this has been discussed before but this is the first problem I encountered starting out as a beginner. how are you guys trying to verify your labelling techniques on the the bigger 4349 reports

Great question. We have 3 choices
* use 58 gold labels
* use our 4.2k created labels from reports
* use the public LB

I've tried numerous combinations of LLMs, but the performance consistently plateaus at around 0.89. I suspect this might be the actual capability ceiling for LLMs. Furthermore, in real-world scenarios, different doctors have varying levels of experience and naturally provide different opinions, meaning the ground truth reports themselves aren't absolutely flawless.

Because of this, I've basically given up on chasing higher metrics. I feel like the ultimate solution might be training multiple models on different labels and relying on trial and error to get better scores. But honestly, this approach feels almost identical to continuous ensembling, which inevitably leads to overfitting.
what is the 0.89 figure exactly?

I got this email about accoutn ban:
```
Hi Jiwei Liu,
Our automated content review system recently found that your content is not compliant with one or more of our policies. See below for more information about your content status and how to correct the issue.

Content:
Notebook: RSNA Knee M1 C9 MaxSpan Inductor cache T4 (2026-08-27 08:10)

Source of Report:Automated systems
Issue Found: Violates our Community Guidelines and/or Termsagainst Resource abuse. For further explanation of why the content and/or use of the platform is considered violative on these grounds, please refer to Kaggle’s Community Guidelines.
Result: We have unpublished the content and issued a ban on your account, unless we determine otherwise after an appeal.
```

The notebook referenced is a simple python script:
```
"""Build a reusable T4 TorchInductor cache for the M1-C9 MaxSpan graph."""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import importlib.metadata
import importlib.util
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import platform
import shutil
import sys
import tarfile
import time


REFERENCE_PARENT_MANIFEST_SHA256 = (
    "e71afd1717aa9c2751a7eafc36960c480a7f10f1da841d26d53cd331b47e51fd"
)


def sha256_file(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for block in iter(lambda: handle.read(8 << 20), b""):
            digest.update(block)
    return digest.hexdigest()


def package() -> Path:
    paths = sorted(
        path.resolve()
        for path in Path("/kaggle/input").glob("**/m0_c3_manifest.json")
        if path.is_file()
    )
    if len(paths) != 1:
        raise FileNotFoundError(
            f"expected one m0_c3_manifest.json, observed {len(paths)}"
        )
    return paths[0].parent


def import_file(name: str, path: Path):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
    if spec is None or spec.loader is None:
        raise RuntimeError(f"cannot import runtime: {path}")
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module


def main() -> None:
    work = Path("/kaggle/working")
    cache = Path("/tmp/torchinductor_cache")
    cache.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR"] = str(cache)
    os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_FX_GRAPH_CACHE"] = "1"
    os.environ["TORCHINDUCTOR_AUTOGRAD_CACHE"] = "1"

    import numpy as np
    import torch

    if torch.cuda.device_count() != 2:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"cache builder requires two visible GPUs, observed "
            f"{torch.cuda.device_count()}"
        )
    gpu_names = [torch.cuda.get_device_name(index) for index in range(2)]
    if any("T4" not in name for name in gpu_names):
        raise RuntimeError(f"cache builder requires T4 GPUs, observed {gpu_names}")

    parent = package()
    manifest_path = parent / "m0_c3_manifest.json"
    manifest_hash = sha256_file(manifest_path)
    if manifest_hash != REFERENCE_PARENT_MANIFEST_SHA256:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"parent manifest drift: expected={REFERENCE_PARENT_MANIFEST_SHA256} "
            f"observed={manifest_hash}"
        )
    manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text())
    checkpoint = parent / "maxspan_member0.pth"
    checkpoint_hash = sha256_file(checkpoint)
    expected_checkpoint_hash = manifest["files"].get(checkpoint.name)
    if checkpoint_hash != expected_checkpoint_hash:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"checkpoint drift: expected={expected_checkpoint_hash} "
            f"observed={checkpoint_hash}"
        )

    runtime_path = parent / "maxspan_runtime.py"
    runtime_hash = sha256_file(runtime_path)
    expected_runtime_hash = manifest["files"].get(runtime_path.name)
    if runtime_hash != expected_runtime_hash:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"runtime drift: expected={expected_runtime_hash} "
            f"observed={runtime_hash}"
        )
    runtime = import_file("m1_c9_fast_maxspan_runtime", runtime_path)

    device_audits = []
    for index in range(2):
        device = torch.device(f"cuda:{index}")
        torch.cuda.set_device(device)
        torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats(index)
        model = runtime.load_model(checkpoint, device)
        image = torch.zeros(
            (
                1,
                runtime.EVAL_WINDOWS,
                3,
                runtime.MODEL_SIZE,
                runtime.MODEL_SIZE,
            ),
            dtype=torch.float32,
            device=device,
        )

        def invoke(candidate):
            with torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast(
                "cuda", dtype=torch.float16
            ):
                return candidate(image).float()

        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        eager_started = time.monotonic()
        eager = invoke(model)
        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        eager_seconds = time.monotonic() - eager_started

        compiled = torch.compile(
            model,
            backend="inductor",
            mode="default",
            fullgraph=False,
            dynamic=False,
        )
        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        compile_started = time.monotonic()
        compiled_first = invoke(compiled)
        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        compile_first_seconds = time.monotonic() - compile_started

        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        steady_started = time.monotonic()
        compiled_steady = invoke(compiled)
        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)
        steady_seconds = time.monotonic() - steady_started
        eager_values = eager.detach().cpu().numpy()
        first_values = compiled_first.detach().cpu().numpy()
        steady_values = compiled_steady.detach().cpu().numpy()
        device_audits.append(
            {
                "device": index,
                "name": gpu_names[index],
                "eager_seconds": eager_seconds,
                "compile_first_seconds": compile_first_seconds,
                "compiled_steady_seconds": steady_seconds,
                "max_abs_compiled_vs_eager": float(
                    np.max(np.abs(first_values - eager_values))
                ),
                "max_abs_compiled_repeat": float(
                    np.max(np.abs(steady_values - first_values))
                ),
                "peak_reserved_bytes": torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved(index),
            }
        )
        del compiled_steady, compiled_first, eager, image, compiled, model
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()

    archive = work / "m1_c9_maxspan_inductor_cache_t4.tar.gz"
    with tarfile.open(archive, "w:gz", compresslevel=6) as handle:
        handle.add(cache, arcname=cache.name)
```

title: Title: Building an open analytics companion for this competition — what would you want in it?

messages.text:
Hi everyone,

Quick intro to what I'm working on, and a genuine ask for your input.

The problem this competition puts in front of us A si![]ngle knee MRI can carry a dozen different findings at once — ACL and MCL injuries, meniscus tears, osteoarthritis, effusion, synovitis, Baker's cyst, contusion, fracture. We're scoring on macro-averaged AUC across all of them, plus a separate efficiency track. That combination is unusual: a model can look strong on the aggregate number and still be quietly weak on two or three findings that happen to be rare. And the efficiency track means the fastest path to a better score isn't always a bigger model.

The leaderboard tells you where you are. It never tells you why.

What I'm building In the last Kaggle competition I entered, I built a free open-source analytics tool for replays. It ended up being used by people from 51 countries in the final weeks, and the biggest lesson was simple: competitors don't want another score, they want to understand their own model.

So I'm building the same idea for this one — a free, no-sign-up, open-source companion where you upload your predictions and immediately see:

Per-finding performance, so you know which of the 12 targets is dragging your macro AUC down
Your hardest cases: where the model is confidently wrong
Threshold and calibration behaviour per target
Efficiency trade-offs: accuracy gained versus runtime spent
Run-to-run comparison, so you can tell a real improvement from noise
Everything runs in your browser. Nothing gets uploaded or stored.

The ask It isn't finished, and that's on purpose. I'd rather build what you actually need than guess.

What would genuinely help you in the next few weeks? A view, a metric, a plot, a sanity check you keep doing by hand? Drop it in the comments and I'll work through the list publicly — I shipped one new feature per day in the last competition and plan to do the same here.

Where to reach me

Right here in the comments — I'll work through every suggestion publicly.
On X: @lopeznomar — I post daily build updates there.
By email: lopeznomar@gmail.com
The app itself is in the works — as soon as it's live, this thread gets the link, and the best ideas from this conversation become the first features.                                                                                                             
Good luck to everyone. 🦵

Independent open-source project. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Kaggle or RSNA.

(https://www.googleapis.com/download/storage/v1/b/kaggle-forum-message-attachments/o/inbox%2F812296%2F1d1a6e3cd2b4892a9bb835c0ec7e326d%2Frsna-knee-ops-lab-intro-clean.png?generation=1790157292685080&alt=media)

Update 9/7/2026 at 11:51 EST - Time down from 2 hours to 29 minutes
@dreaddevelopment Thanks for all your contributions. I am currently using your labels. And I have read your notebooks and discussions for ideas.

Thanks for publishing these, and for the geometry table on the dataset pages - it's what makes them usable without burning submissions to guess. We run maxspan-v5 and native384dense-v10 as a two-arm blend over a shared decode.

A question about the one page that omits the geometry. Nine of the ten Raptor datasets state slices / span / crop / stored px; raptor-knee-finespacing says only "the Fine Spacing preprocessing of the corpus". Given your note above that the later corpora "go to 80-96 slices", I'd rather not feed v9 a volume it never saw:

1. What slice count and span does the Fine Spacing corpus use?

2. Was the 0.932 scored at your 94 windows per study, or at a lower count?

The reason for (2) is your own fullspan result: widening the span at a fixed 44 slices cost 0.009, with the conclusion that widening only pays if slices are added to keep the sampling dense. If Fine Spacing is a 96-slice corpus, then scoring it on a 64-slot volume at 62 windows is that same density mismatch in the same direction - so the 0.932 wouldn't be available at 62 windows, and the checkpoint swap and the window count would be two different levers rather than one.

Also, if you happen to remember: "42 windows got 0.930" for the trimmed run - was that on the Fine Spacing corpus or the 64-slice one?

Happy to report back what we measure either way.

Good catch. That page went up without the geometry line and I've just fixed it, so it's on the dataset now along with a note about window counts.
Fine Spacing is 80 slices per study across 2 to 98 percent of each series, a 140 mm crop, stored at 336 pixels. The slots are 22 sagittal fluid, 18 sagittal, 15 coronal fluid, 10 coronal, 15 axial. Full window coverage is 78.
The 0.932 was scored at 78, so no, it isn't available at 62, and your reasoning about why is right. Same effect as the full span result: 44 slices over 2 to 98 percent scored 0.917 against 0.926 for 44 over 6 to 94, so spreading the same slices thinner cost 0.009. Putting 64 slices over the wide span brought it to 0.928, and 80 slices to 0.932. Density is the lever rather than span, and 1.20 percent of the stack per slice is the finest I've measured and also the best. Scoring an 80 slice volume at 62 windows leaves about a fifth of it unread, and at that point the checkpoint swap and the coverage change stop being separable, which is exactly what you said.
On the 42 window 0.930, I think two numbers from this thread have got stuck together. My 42 window results top out at 0.926. The 0.924 is the 64 slice corpus at 42 windows, and the identical weights read 0.927 at 62. The 0.930 is Jack's, further up this thread, from running the widedense SWA checkpoint with more coverage than my original run used.
Please do report back what you get, I'd be interested either way.

Reporting back as promised. Your density curve doesn't transfer to our pipeline, and I think the reason is instructive.
We tested it at fixed everything-else on one fold: 8 slices/slot → 10 slices/slot, which on our 0.12–0.88 band moves us from 1.58% to 1.27% of the stack per slice into the range you measured as best. It came back −0.0045 (plateau −0.0046) against a 0.003 noise threshold, so a real, small negative. We also tried tightening the crop 140 → 110 mm at the denser sampling: +0.0005, inside noise, unresolved.
The difference is probably structural rather than a contradiction. You sample 80 slices across whole series and score every window position, so extra slices buy genuinely new coverage. We sample 6 per-series slots into a masked attention head that pools 48 tokens, so extra slices mostly dilute the softmax rather than adding field of view the head already sees the whole span, just coarsely. Density is a coverage lever for you and a pooling-composition change for us.
Two other one-variable results from the same week, in case they're useful: swapping RadImageNet for ImageNet ResNet-50 at identical architecture and correct per-corpus normalisation cost us −0.063, and replacing our attention head with masked mean pooling cost −0.014. So for this pipeline the medical pretraining and the learned pooling are both doing real work.
Thanks again for publishing the geometry it saved us from spending a submission finding out that 0.932 wasn't available at 62 windows.

Thats a clean result & I think your read on it is right.

Worth knowing from this side, the lever has a ceiling for us too.
Going from 48-72 eval windows , a 50% increase moved the board 0.944 & cost 8 minutes of runtime. So it isnt that density pays for me & not for you, its that it stops paying & in your setup it stop paying earlier then goes slightly negative.

Coverage lever versus pooling compositon  change is exactly the distinction. If the head already sees the whole span, extra slices arent new information, they're more tokens competing in the same softmax & past some point thats a cost rather than a gain.

One that does go the other way for you is RadImageNet, that was a negative in my pipeline.

And your masked mean result matches something I saw from the other direction, changing the pooling at inference on weights that were trained with attention cost about 0.02. The heads weighting is not a formality.

thank you greatly for reporting back properly with the noise threshold attached. rare <3

That framing helps a lot "more tokens competing in the same softmax" predicts the shape we got, not just the sign. Our coverage curve over 4,407 studies, weak-label macro, shipped heads, nothing retrained:

k=16  0.8867     k=40  0.8934  (+0.0002 vs k=31)
k=24  0.8909     k=48  0.8939  (+0.0007)
k=31  0.8932     k=56  0.8940  (+0.0008)
k=62  0.8948  (+0.0016)

So it climbs to ~31 and then flattens for the next 30 windows. Noise floor on this ruler is ~0.002, so everything from 40 to 62 is one flat line with a slight upward drift at the end. That matches your 48→72 reading the density lever isn't differently-signed between us, it's just that we're further along the same saturating curve. Caveat on my side: those checkpoints were trained on these studies, so the absolute level is inflated; the shape is what I'd trust, not the number.

On RadImageNet going the other way I think I can offer a mechanism, because it was negative for us too until one change. Fold-0, out-of-fold, n=1102:

ImageNet ResNet-34,   3 adjacent slices as channels   0.8152
RadImageNet R50,      3 adjacent slices as channels   0.8339
RadImageNet R50,      centre slice repeated x3        0.8542

The trunk swap alone was worth +0.019. The channel contract was worth another +0.020 on its own. RadImageNet is pretrained on single-channel medical images replicated across RGB, so a 2.5D stack of adjacent slices is out-of-distribution for its first conv in a way ImageNet weights don't care about ImageNet was trained on real colour. If your pipeline fed it a slice triplet (which any Raptor-geometry setup naturally does), that's likely most of your negative. Costs one line to test.

Same family as your pooling point, now that I look at it: both are cases where the weights carry an input contract that isn't in the config, and violating it reads as "that component doesn't work here."

One disagreement worth flagging, since it's your shipped config: the reversed arm measures negative on our ruler. v5 forward 0.8943 vs reversed 0.8873, and adding both reversals takes the blend from 0.8948 to 0.8918. Your stack weights maxspan-v5-reverse at 0.10, so either our ruler disagrees with the board, or it earns its place through decorrelation inside a bigger ensemble than the two arms I'm testing it in. I'd believe the second just recording that I couldn't reproduce it as a standalone gain.
One more, unrelated but cheap: coatnet_rmlp_2 accepts img_size=256 with the 384 checkpoint and zero missing tensors, strict=True passes, 2.9× faster. It also loses 0.029 AUC. The rmlp bias generalises architecturally and not functionally  the tensors fit, the features don't survive.

title: Multimodal Fusion Bottlenecks: Aligning 3D MRI Volume Embeddings with Multilingual Report Transformers

messages.text:
## Introduction:

Hi all,
As the leaderboard accelerates past 0.95, I’ve been experimenting with the multimodal aspect of the RSNA Knee Abnormality Detection dataset. While visual-only backbones give a solid baseline, properly fusing the 3D MRIs with the multi-language text reports presents a unique architecture bottleneck.

I wanted to share a specific roadblock I hit regarding cross-attention alignment, along with a lightweight fusion snippet, to see how others are tackling this.


## The Roadblock / Insight

When feeding the 3D MRI embeddings (extracted via a 3D-EfficientNet) and text embeddings (via a multilingual BERT variant) into a late-fusion Cross-Attention layer, I noticed a severe gradient imbalance. The model aggressively overfits to the text reports within the first 3 epochs, completely ignoring subtle visual cues for rarer abnormalities like MCL tears.
To mitigate this, I implemented a custom Layer-wise Learning Rate Decay (LLRD) specifically for the text encoder to prevent it from dominating early training.

## Quick preview of the Multimodal Cross-Attention Block I am testing

`

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class RSNAKneeFusion(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, visual_dim=1024, text_dim=768, embed_dim=512):
        super().__init__()
        self.vis_proj = nn.Linear(visual_dim, embed_dim)
        self.txt_proj = nn.Linear(text_dim, embed_dim)
        self.cross_attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim, num_heads=8, batch_first=True)
        
    def forward(self, image_feats, text_feats):
        # image_feats shape: [B, S, 1024] (3D context tokens)
        # text_feats shape:  [B, T, 768]  (Radiology report tokens)
        v = self.vis_proj(image_feats)
        t = self.txt_proj(text_feats)
        
        # Query: Image, Key/Value: Text
        attn_out, _ = self.cross_attn(v, t, t)
        return attn_out.mean(dim=1) # Global fused representation
`

###The Peer-Level Questions :

Q1 ) Text Bias: Is anyone else finding that multimodal models overfit drastically faster than vision-only models on this dataset? Are you utilizing a warm-up strategy for the image backbone before introducing text?

Q2) Tokenization: With the reports being in a dozen different languages, did you find standard translation APIs helpful, or are native multilingual models (like XLM-RoBERTa) retaining the clinical nuances better?

Q3) CV-to-LB Correlation: My local 5-fold CV tracks perfectly with the text-dominant model, but I suspect a private LB shakeup if the hidden test set contains missing or brief text reports. How are you handling potential missing text modalities at inference?

have you tried to completely freeze the text encoder and train just the image encoder? This way, you don't need reports in testing. you are just using them to get a study-wise embedding that you can later train with a small set of high-quality labels. This is an idea I was contemplating.

title: Why ~200 public forks sit at exactly 0.941

messages.text:
The bigger point is that basically **no one besides [@DreadDevelopment](https://www.kaggle.com/dreaddevelopment) and me has released genuinely new models recently**.

Building a new model, prototyping it, training it and running proper ablations takes hours or days. Changing `0.55/0.15` to `0.60/0.10`, re-ranking, or tweaking per-label blend weights takes minutes.

Repeat those minute-scale changes across dozens or hundreds of submissions and you are simply overfitting the public LB. A `.940 → .941` move from another blend tweak is not strong evidence of a better model.

That is also why I would be very cautious about reading too much into whether 0.55/0.15 or 0.60/0.10 is “better.” Without new models or an independent validation signal, repeatedly searching those blend weights is basically another hyperparameter search on the public split.

Some of this is probably encouraged by the incentive to reach the top of the public leaderboard and make popular notebooks, but that is different from demonstrating better generalization on the hidden test.

Around 200 teams share a public score of exactly 0.941, and most run a fork of @mattiaangeli's *Bend the Knee to the Dinosaurs* with the 0.941 recipe from @maverickss26 / @renta0426. I diffed the forks against the base and found three things worth knowing if you're in that block.

**1. The base notebook documents its own experiments.** Its `.ipynb` metadata holds an `rsna_optimization` entry per version, naming the single predictive change each version made. Pull the notebook with `kaggle kernels pull mattiaangeli/bend-the-knee-to-the-dinosaurs -m` and read the metadata of the JSON file. It's the closest thing to an ablation log this competition has.

**2. The 0.941 recipe is three changes, not four.** Against v27 (0.940) it changes the per-label outer CoAt weights, re-ranks the inner CoAt/Raptor hybrid, sets the Raptor arms to 0.55/0.15, and re-ranks `_ke_cr`. That last one does nothing: `_raptor.csv` is already a percentile rank at that point.

**3. Mattia's own stack keeps the Raptor arms at 0.60/0.10.** His ledger shows the per-label map and the inner re-rank adopted, but not the 0.55/0.15 arms. Every 0.55/0.15 build I could find (maverickss26, renta0426, mine, a public copy of mine) sits at 0.941, and @jiweiliu's speed fork independently reverted the same two weights.

Every number here is a real submission:

| configuration | public |
|---|---|
| v27, `model_sources`/`kernel_sources` missing (all 20 DINOv2 members silently dropped) | 0.937 |
| v27, complete sources | 0.940 |
| + per-label map, inner re-rank, arms 0.55/0.15 | 0.941 |
| + arms back to 0.60/0.10 | [SCORE] |

A runnable version with the full source checklist is here: https://www.kaggle.com/code/starkhushi/rsna-knee-why-public-forks-stop-at-0-941

One caveat: the per-label map was tuned on the public split, and `Lateral Meniscus = 1.00` discards three of the four stages for that column. Keep a flat-0.60 version as your second final pick.

title: Fluid_Sensitive and Fat_Suppression appear identical across all series

messages.text:
This question is best addressed at a general level rather than as a statement about how participants should interpret this specific dataset. Part of the challenge is understanding the characteristics of the training data and how the diagnostic space represented here relates to the broader complexity of musculoskeletal MRI. Any curated dataset is necessarily a subset of the real world, and even carefully defined features may not capture every combination or edge case encountered in clinical practice.

Fat suppression, whether achieved by inversion recovery, frequency-selective fat saturation, or another technique, is not inherently the same as fluid sensitivity.

In musculoskeletal MRI, however, the two can and often do occur together. Fluid-sensitive sequences commonly highlight edema, hemorrhage/contusion, and other abnormalities in soft tissues and bone marrow. Because subcutaneous tissues and bone marrow contain substantial amounts of fat, suppressing the fat signal generally makes these fluid-related abnormalities easier to visualize. 

As a result, most clinically useful fluid-sensitive MSK sequences are also fat-suppressed.

That relationship is not absolute. A fluid-sensitive sequence does not necessarily have to be fat-suppressed, and a fat-suppressed sequence is not necessarily fluid-sensitive. For example, when evaluating bone tumors or musculoskeletal infection, fat-suppressed non-fluid-sensitive sequences may be used before and after contrast administration so enhancement can be assessed directly.

Accordingly, while the two columns appear identical across the current training dataset, they represent conceptually distinct imaging characteristics. Their equality in the training data should not be interpreted as meaning the terms are generally interchangeable in MRI, or that they must be equal in another dataset.

title: Six data traps in RSNA Knee: slice order, missing laterality, silent reports (EDA)

messages.text:
I published an EDA that tries to answer one question: what does this data force a model to do? 
https://www.kaggle.com/code/gchauhan/eda-rsna-knee-what-the-data-tells-us

**What stood out**

- Training targets come from reports; the score comes from radiologists reading images. On the 58 expert-labelled studies, reports are silent on about half of the expert-positive Synovitis cases. Fracture is in 7% of reports but 31% of expert labels. Treating "not mentioned" as "absent" teaches the model the reporting habit, not the finding.
- InstanceNumber runs against slice position in over a third of series. If you stack slices by instance number, neighbouring-slice context is scrambled for those series. Sort by position along the slice normal.
- Laterality is missing in about half of studies. Work out the side from geometry before mirroring right knees to left. If you flip for augmentation, medial/lateral labels (menisci, OA) have to swap too.
- The CSV hides the contrast. "non-FS" mixes T1, PD and T2, and most repeated series types are a second contrast rather than a retake. Keying slots only on plane × FS merges different images.
- A study is a variable set of 3–14 series. The most common combination covers only 40% of studies, so a missing-series mask isn't optional.
- Slices are ~10× farther apart than pixels (~0.3 mm in-plane vs ~3.5 mm between slices). That favours 2.5D, meaning a 2D encoder plus a depth model, over 3D from scratch, which is also what past RSNA spine/PE winners found.

The last section maps each finding to a modelling consequence and to what winners of past RSNA imaging competitions did.

Report labels are from @pilkwang's LLM-read report labels (https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/pilkwang/rsna-knee-llm-labels). Thanks!

title: Winner's obligations when the submitted weights are a public checkpoint someone else trained

messages.text:
Section 2.8.a requires a winner to deliver "training code, inference code, model weights" and to publish the weights as a public Kaggle dataset. Section 2.6 separately permits freely and publicly available pretrained models, and the Code Requirements page states this explicitly.
Those two are clear individually but not in combination. Consider a submission whose predictions come entirely from a publicly available checkpoint that another participant trained and released, used without modification. The participant's own contribution is the inference pipeline preprocessing, windowing, aggregation, runtime engineering not the weights.
1. Can such a submission be eligible for a Leaderboard or Efficiency Prize?
2. If so, what satisfies the training-code obligation pointing to the original author's published training code, or must the winner have trained the weights themselves?
Section 2.8.a.a carves out commercially available software that the Sponsor can procure without undue expense, but says nothing about model weights, which is where the ambiguity sits.
This matters most for the Efficiency Track, where a single strong public checkpoint plus a fast inference pipeline is a natural approach, and asking now avoids discovering the answer at the Nov 5 deadline.

title: The leaderboard shows 3 decimals and I spent 20 submissions inside one of them

messages.text: Thank you for the leaderboard showing 3 decimals @zhincez

I blended a public notebook with my own CoAtNet ensemble, then spent two weeks tuning the blend. Here is the whole weight sweep with the leaderboard score each one produced. W is the weight on the public source, rank-mean blending.

```
W_pub   LB
0.00   0.934   (pure my own ensemble)
0.15   0.935
0.30   0.936
0.45   0.936
0.50   0.937
0.60   0.937
0.70   0.937
0.75   0.937
0.90   0.936
1.00   0.936   (pure public notebook)
```

Ten points on the axis, four distinct numbers, and a flat plateau from 0.50 to 0.75.

Then I changed the blend operator instead of the weight, all at W = 0.60:

```
rank-mean                 0.937
probability space         0.937
logit space               0.937
geometric mean on rank    0.937
power mean, order 2       0.936
rank clipped to [.05,.95] 0.937
```

Then adaptive weights: per study, per label, twelve separate coefficients, the same thing with the sign flipped, a version with double the span. Every one of them: 0.937.

Counting up, 13 of my submissions read exactly 0.937 and I cannot order any of them.

The part worth sitting with: pure public is 0.936 and pure mine is 0.934, so everything my own ensemble adds on top of a public notebook is worth at most one displayed digit. Two weeks of blend tuning bought me 0.001, and I have no idea whether that 0.001 is real or rounding.

I do not have a clean answer, but two things I would do differently:

Check the display resolution against the effect size before starting an axis. Three decimals means anything under about 0.0005 is invisible, and blend weight moves the score by less than that across most of its range. That axis was never measurable here, no matter how many submissions I threw at it.

Build the local ruler first. Mine ran the wrong way: my 58-study gold set ranked variants in roughly the opposite order to the leaderboard, so I had no way to break the ties either. I kept submitting because the leaderboard was the only number I had, which is exactly backwards.

If anyone has a local validation setup that actually correlates with the board here, I would like to hear how you built it. Especially how you split, given how few studies carry the rarer labels.

title: Metric edge cases: single-class label columns, and corrupted DICOMs in the test set

messages.text:
Good questions. I would handle both cases defensively in the submission:

1. For a single-class label, do not assume that the scorer skips the column or substitutes 0.5. In local validation, `roc_auc_score` is undefined for a single class, so the exact competition behavior should be confirmed by the host.

2. For corrupted DICOMs, wrap `pixel_array` in a guarded loader, log the failure, and use a deterministic fallback such as a neighboring valid slice or a zero-filled image. This prevents one malformed study from crashing the entire submission.

Until the host confirms the scorer behavior and test-data guarantees, treating both cases defensively is the safest approach.

Two narrow questions about how the evaluation behaves in edge cases. Both change
how a submission is built, so I would rather ask than guess.

1. Single-class label columns.
   The metric is the unweighted mean of 12 per-label ROC AUCs. If one of the 12
   label columns happens to contain only one class in the private test set, what
   does the scorer do with it: skip that column and average over the remaining
   ones, substitute 0.5, or does the submission error out? With 12 labels and the
   rarer findings this seems worth pinning down, because "skip" and "substitute
   0.5" give materially different macro scores for the same predictions.

2. Corrupted DICOMs in the test set.
   Two threads report training studies whose PixelData is truncated relative to
   the Group 0028 header, so pydicom raises ValueError on .pixel_array
   (discussion/738708 and discussion/737163). Are the test studies known to be
   free of this, or should submissions be written to survive it? A single
   unhandled file would turn a working submission into a zero, so if the test set
   is not guaranteed clean it would help everyone to say so explicitly.

Thanks!
